sbh1.3:1.1: What is the stage of renunciation?
sbh1.3:1.3: the going to dispassion by the worldly path,
sbh1.3:1.4: the going to dispassion by the supramundane path,
sbh1.3:1.5: and the requisites for these two — gathered into one, this is called the stage of renunciation.
sbh1.3:1.6: What is going to dispassion by the worldly path?
sbh1.3:1.7: When someone here sees coarseness in the realm of desire,
sbh1.3:1.8: and sees peacefulness in the first dhyāna — both as a meditative attainment and as a [corresponding] mode of rebirth — born of seclusion, accompanied by joy and pleasure:
sbh1.3:1.9: so seeing, abiding much in that, he attains dispassion toward the [desire-realm] personality,
sbh1.3:1.11: So, above each dhyāna, he becomes a seer of coarseness in all the lower stages
sbh1.3:1.12: and a seer of peacefulness in all the upper stages; so seeing, abiding much in that, he attains dispassion all the way up to the sphere of nothingness,
sbh1.3:1.13: And he attains the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
sbh1.3:1.14: The going to dispassion by the worldly path goes no higher, no further than this.
sbh1.3:1.15: What is the going to dispassion by the supramundane path?
sbh1.3:1.16: When someone here, having seen good persons, learned in the noble dharmas, truly knows suffering as suffering,
sbh1.3:1.21: thereafter, cultivating the higher path, he disjoins and releases himself from the dharmas of the three realms — those to be abandoned by [the path of] vision and [the path of] cultivation — and thus passes beyond the three realms.
sbh1.3:1.22: This is called going to dispassion by the supramundane path.
sbh1.3:2.3: wholesome dharma-desire, restraint of virtue, [restraint of] sense-faculties, knowing the right measure in food, application to wakefulness in the early and late watches of the night, dwelling with full awareness, association with good friends, hearing-and-reflection on the true dharma, [practice] without obstacle, generosity, the ornament of the recluse — these dharmas are called the requisites for going to worldly and supramundane dispassion.
sbh1.3:2.4: Of these, endowment-from-self, endowment-from-others, and wholesome dharma-desire — their division is to be understood as before,
sbh1.3:2.5: namely as stated [in the gotrabhūmi] regarding the lesser supporting condition for the perfecting of the seed.
sbh1.3:2.7: When someone here dwells endowed with virtue, [and so on through the standard formula] up through undertaking the precepts of training.
sbh1.3:2.8: How, again, does he dwell endowed with virtue?
sbh1.3:2.9: [As above,] up through undertaking the precepts of training.
sbh1.3:2.10: How [more concretely] does he dwell endowed with virtue?
sbh1.3:2.11: When, in the precepts undertaken, his bodily action is unimpaired,
sbh1.3:2.12: his conduct unbroken, his conduct unrent — thus is he endowed with virtue.
sbh1.3:3.1: How is he restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa?
sbh1.3:3.2: The seven categories of virtue conducive to liberation are called the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.
sbh1.3:3.3: These same restraints, divided by category, are many.
sbh1.3:3.4: Here, however, taking the monastic [bhikṣu] restraint specifically, [the text] says ‘restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.’
sbh1.3:3.5: How is he endowed with proper conduct?
sbh1.3:3.6: When, undertaking deportment, duties-to-be-performed, or application to the wholesome side, he is endowed with conduct that does not transgress the world and does not transgress the Vinaya.
sbh1.3:3.8: How does he avoid transgressing the world and avoid transgressing the Vinaya [in this respect]?
sbh1.3:3.9: He walks where one should walk,
sbh1.3:3.10: and walks as one should walk —
sbh1.3:3.11: [walking] in such a way that he is not blamed by the world, by the good, by the rightly delighted, by the noble ones, by his co-religionists, by the Vinaya-holders, by those trained in Vinaya; he is not censurable,
sbh1.3:3.12: not in a position to be reproached.
sbh1.3:3.13: As with walking, so with standing, sitting, and lying down — [the same applies].
sbh1.3:3.15: How does he avoid transgressing the world,
sbh1.3:3.16: [how does he avoid] transgressing the Vinaya? — [These] are called the duties-to-be-performed:
sbh1.3:3.19: [the use of] water and the tooth-stick,
sbh1.3:3.21: taking and bringing back alms-food, eating,
sbh1.3:3.22: the cleaning and putting away of the bowl,
sbh1.3:3.24: the laying out of the lodging —
sbh1.3:3.25: and, in summary, bowl-work and robe-work.
sbh1.3:3.26: Whatever else is of this kind is called a duty-to-be-performed.
sbh1.3:3.27: These, as appropriate — wherever they are to be performed and however they are to be performed — he performs there and in that manner,
sbh1.3:3.28: such that he is not criticized by worldlings, not censured;
sbh1.3:3.29: by the Vinaya-holders and those trained in Vinaya, he is not blameworthy, not censured;
sbh1.3:3.30: by the rightly delighted co-religionists [likewise]. Thus conduct grounded in duties-to-be-performed is conduct that does not transgress the world
sbh1.3:3.31: and does not transgress the Vinaya.
sbh1.3:4.1: [Third,] conduct grounded in application to the wholesome side.
sbh1.3:4.2: How is this non-transgressive of the world and non-transgressive of the Vinaya?
sbh1.3:4.3: The wholesome side is said to be:
sbh1.3:4.4: attending and serving the recitation-teachers, looking after the sick, mutually arousing compassionate mind, the exchange of consents [chanda-dāna], inquiry, hearing of Dharma, adroitness in service, performing bodily and verbal duties toward co-religionists, rousing others to the wholesome side, teaching Dharma,
sbh1.3:4.5: entering retreat, sitting cross-legged — these and other such dharmas are called
sbh1.3:4.7: He, accordingly — as has been proclaimed,
sbh1.3:4.8: wherever it is to be performed — performs it in just that way,
sbh1.3:4.9: such that he is not blameworthy,
sbh1.3:4.10: not censured by worldlings, by Vinaya-holders, by those trained in Vinaya, by the rightly delighted, by the noble persons, or by his co-religionists. This is called conduct grounded in application to the wholesome side, [conduct] non-transgressive of world and Vinaya.
sbh1.3:4.11: One endowed with such modes of conduct is called endowed with proper conduct.
sbh1.3:4.12: Thus he is endowed with proper conduct.
sbh1.3:4.13: And how is he endowed with proper resort?
sbh1.3:4.14: Five are the non-resorts for a monk.
sbh1.3:4.16: The brothel, the entertainer’s place, the tavern, the royal household, and fifth the caṇḍāla [outcaste] execution-ground.
sbh1.3:4.17: He who avoids these non-resorts rejected by the Tathāgata, and who at the right time frequents elsewhere — the blameless resort — is endowed with proper resort.
sbh1.3:5.1: How does he see danger in the slightest fault?
sbh1.3:5.2: ‘Slightest fault’ is so called [for the following reasons].
sbh1.3:5.3: Very minor are those precepts of training in which transgression and rising-out [from transgression] are recognized [as small].
sbh1.3:5.4: Transgression of those [minor precepts] is the slightest fault.
sbh1.3:5.5: Again, since rising-out from such transgression is accomplished with little difficulty, it is therefore called slightest.
sbh1.3:5.6: How, then, does he see danger [in it]?
sbh1.3:5.7: He reflects: ‘On account of this transgression I would become unfit for the attainment of the not-yet-attained, for the realization of the not-realized, for the direct touching of the not-yet-touched; I would go to the lower realms, would become one bound for the lower realms; I would reproach myself, or the Teacher would reproach me, or the deities, or the wise, or my co-religionists would censure me as acting contrary to Dharma;
sbh1.3:5.8: and in all directions and intermediate directions an evil reputation would arise about me’ — through [reflection on] the visible-here-and-now consequences and the after-state consequences, and through the distinguished dharmas obstructed by them, he becomes one who sees danger.
sbh1.3:5.9: By this [seeing of danger] he does not violate even those very minor precepts of training even for the sake of life — under any circumstance.
sbh1.3:5.10: If at some time, on some occasion, through forgetfulness he transgresses, he confesses [it] lightly, very lightly, according to Dharma, and rises out [of the transgression].
sbh1.3:5.11: Thus he sees danger in the slightest fault.
sbh1.3:5.12: How does he train by undertaking the precepts of training?
sbh1.3:5.14: Previously, when receiving the Prātimokṣa-restraint by the fourth formal act of motion at his full ordination, he heard the formulation of only a few precepts; the further hundred-odd precepts of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra he received only by way of pledge, [saying] ‘I shall acquire them in all respects.’
sbh1.3:5.15: Having heard from his preceptor and instructor the Prātimokṣa-sūtra recited in the standard formula — addressed [to him], esteemed, and beloved —
sbh1.3:5.16: by which [recitation] the Prātimokṣa-restraint [is to be received] through the undertaking of all the trainings — [though] his intellect [had] not [yet] awakened [to them in detail]:
sbh1.3:5.17: those precepts previously undertaken by way of pledge he now undertakes through skilled awakening [to their actual content],
sbh1.3:5.18: [doing so] on the basis previously proclaimed, [namely] from the preceptor or instructor, as before.
sbh1.3:5.19: And having thus undertaken [them] through skilled awakening, he trains as instructed, neither lessening nor adding.
sbh1.3:5.20: In those precepts of training proclaimed in the Teacher’s place [i.e., authoritatively transmitted], he is a non-perverted grasper both as to meaning and as to letter.
sbh1.3:5.21: Thus he trains by undertaking the precepts of training. — Such, in this much, is the detailed division of the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:6.1: What, then, is the summary meaning?
sbh1.3:6.2: This summary meaning has just three marks.
sbh1.3:6.3: [That is,] the aggregate of virtue is elucidated by the Blessed One under three marks: the mark of non-loss, the mark of own-nature, and the mark of own-nature-with-its-qualities.
sbh1.3:6.4: How so? — In that he says ‘he dwells endowed with virtue,’ by this the non-loss mark of the restraint of virtue is declared.
sbh1.3:7.1: In that he says ‘restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa,’
sbh1.3:7.2: by this the own-nature mark is declared.
sbh1.3:7.4: ‘endowed with proper conduct and proper resort,’
sbh1.3:7.5: by this — taking him in further [comparison] — the quality-mark of the Prātimokṣa-restraint so undertaken is declared.
sbh1.3:7.6: For when others gain fullness of conduct and resort, the unbelieving become believing, and the believing gain still greater abundance [of faith];
sbh1.3:7.7: the believing practice for the sake of [further] believing.
sbh1.3:7.8: And they do not defile their minds,
sbh1.3:7.9: they do not generate ill-repute. [Without this,] for one endowed with virtue and endowed with proper conduct and resort, this [further benefit] dependent on others would be a quality and benefit [missed]; in the opposite case, it would in fact be his fault.
sbh1.3:7.11: ‘seeing danger in the slightest faults, he undertakes the precepts of training,’
sbh1.3:7.12: by this the mark of the inner-quality-benefit is declared.
sbh1.3:7.13: For what reason? Because this person, endowed with proper conduct and resort, [already] gains the quality-benefit dependent on others.
sbh1.3:7.15: [were he to] ruin virtue, by that cause, by that condition, he would be reborn in the lower realms,
sbh1.3:7.16: or would become unfit for the attainment of the not-yet-attained, [as detailed] above.
sbh1.3:7.17: Now since he sees danger in the slightest fault —
sbh1.3:7.18: still more in the gross — and trains by undertaking the precepts of training, by that cause, by that condition, at the breaking up of the body he is reborn in a happy destiny,
sbh1.3:7.19: or becomes fit for the attainment of the not-yet-attained, [as] above. For this reason [the foregoing] is called the inner-quality-benefit of the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:8.2: in brief, the Blessed One has elucidated [under three rubrics] undertaken-virtue, outgoing-virtue, and the cultivation of virtue.
sbh1.3:8.4: ‘he dwells endowed with virtue,’ by this undertaken-virtue is declared.
sbh1.3:8.6: ‘restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa,’ by this outgoing-virtue [niḥsaraṇa] is declared.
sbh1.3:8.7: For the virtue subsumed under the Prātimokṣa-restraint is called the training in higher virtue [adhiśīla].
sbh1.3:8.8: And on the basis of the training in higher virtue, he cultivates the training in higher mind [adhicitta] and the training in higher wisdom [adhiprajñā] — and thus is led out toward the destruction of all suffering.
sbh1.3:8.9: He goes forth [from saṁsāra by this means].
sbh1.3:8.10: That is, on the basis of higher virtue, taking it as forerunner — therefore the Prātimokṣa-restraint is called outgoing-virtue.
sbh1.3:8.12: ‘endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, undertaking the precepts of training,’ by this the cultivation of virtue is declared.
sbh1.3:8.13: By these modes that Prātimokṣa-restraint-virtue is to be cultivated,
sbh1.3:8.14: and so cultivated, it becomes well cultivated. Thus this single restraint of virtue is to be understood as set forth by a six-mode teaching.
sbh1.3:9.1: This restraint of virtue is to be understood as ruined by ten modes,
sbh1.3:9.2: and conversely, by ten causes, [as] perfected.
sbh1.3:9.3: By what ten causes is it ruined?
sbh1.3:9.4: It is ill-grasped from the very beginning; it is excessively slack; it is excessively strict; it is gripped by heedlessness and indolence;
sbh1.3:9.6: it is gripped by deficiency of conduct. Here, how is virtue ill-grasped from the very beginning?
sbh1.3:9.7: When someone here goes forth as one resolved upon by a king, or resolved upon by thieves, or distressed by debt, or distressed by fear, or in fear for his livelihood — not for the sake of asceticism, not for the sake of brahminhood [brāhmaṇya], not for the calming of self, not for the restraint of self, not for the final nirvāṇa of self — thus from the very beginning
sbh1.3:9.10: When someone here is shameless, with weak dread of evil [conduct],
sbh1.3:9.11: loose, doing loosely what is taught in the training — this is excessive slackness.
sbh1.3:10.2: When someone here is an ill-grasper, feeling regret in the wrong place —
sbh1.3:10.3: feeling regret in cases where good action is in fact being done;
sbh1.3:10.4: without proper occasion, he produces with respect to others
sbh1.3:10.5: either a contemptuous attitude or a denouncing one — and reports [the supposed faults] to them. Thus it is excessively strict.
sbh1.3:10.6: How is it gripped by heedlessness and indolence?
sbh1.3:10.7: When someone here, with respect to the past, has fallen into transgression,
sbh1.3:10.8: and through forgetfulness has not atoned for a single [transgression] according to Dharma;
sbh1.3:10.9: as with the past, so with the future and the present — whatever transgression he has fallen into,
sbh1.3:10.10: through forgetfulness none is atoned for according to Dharma;
sbh1.3:10.11: and he does not, in advance, undertake intense effort for the sake of non-transgression in the future, [resolving]
sbh1.3:10.12: ‘Let me act in such a way that, acting and dwelling [so], I would not commit transgression’ — yet so he acts, so he dwells,
sbh1.3:10.14: He, with heedlessness regarding past time, future time, and intermediate time — with heedlessness regarding what was to be done in past time — holds dear the pleasure of sleep, of lying down, of side-resting;
sbh1.3:10.15: he becomes unskilled, lazy, lacking energy [to rise up]; he does not perform bodily service for his wise co-religionists. Thus engaged, he is gripped by heedlessness and indolence.
sbh1.3:11.2: When someone here lives the holy life having resolved:
sbh1.3:11.3: ‘By this virtue, observance, austerity, holy life, I shall become a god or some [other] kind of divine being,’ desirous of gain and honor.
sbh1.3:11.4: He seeks gain and honor from others;
sbh1.3:11.5: he yearns for gain and honor.
sbh1.3:11.7: How is it gripped by deficiency of conduct?
sbh1.3:11.8: When someone here, having undertaken either deportment, or duties-to-be-performed, or application to the wholesome side, transgresses the world
sbh1.3:11.9: and transgresses the Vinaya, [as detailed] above — thus it is gripped by deficiency of conduct.
sbh1.3:11.10: How is it gripped by deficiency of livelihood?
sbh1.3:11.11: When someone here is of great desires, discontented, of dull memory, of bad-house lineage [duṣkulīna],
sbh1.3:11.13: not by Dharma — and seeks alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites by non-Dharma,
sbh1.3:11.15: and for the sake of robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — for the sake of generating regard [for himself in others] — he displays to others a contrived, deliberately composed deportment: non-restless faculties, non-fickle faculties, peaceful faculties,
sbh1.3:11.16: by which others, having generated regard for his qualities, think [that things] should be given, [things] should be done —
sbh1.3:11.17: namely, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites.
sbh1.3:11.19: brazen, frivolous, taking note of [people’s] names and clans; he is much-learned,
sbh1.3:11.20: a Dharma-holder, and from a gain-motive alone he speaks Dharma to others — [recounting] what was said by the disciples, or his own qualities, or some past matters, becoming the speaker himself — having attributed something [to himself that does not belong to him].
sbh1.3:11.21: He makes others speak [the offer] by hinting;
sbh1.3:11.22: even when not [being] approached, he points out a robe of ordinary kind, [thinking]: ‘a faithful brāhmaṇa-householder, seeing his deficiency of cloth, will think a great, fine robe is to be given.’
sbh1.3:11.23: As with the robe, so with any other recluse’s requisite — when he does not obtain it at will from faithful brāhmaṇa-householders, or when the enjoyments are non-existent or not present — by importunity he begs,
sbh1.3:11.24: pressing them and speaking harshly. Or, having obtained an inferior thing when [better] enjoyments are present, he derogates that gain, depreciates it,
sbh1.3:11.25: and in front of the giver-patron speaks thus:
sbh1.3:11.26: ‘Ho, son of good family, there are sons of good family and daughters [of good family] in your vicinity — of lower clan and poorer than you — who nevertheless give thus and so, finely, pleasingly.
sbh1.3:11.27: Why do you, of higher clan and other [advantages], not give as pleasingly? Why are you not a pleasing-giver, not a not-meager-not-limited-giver?’
sbh1.3:11.28: He who by such modes — relying on hypocrisy, on talkative chatter [lapanā], on insinuation [naimittikatā], on extortion [naiṣpeṣikatā], on gain-seeking-by-gain [lābhena lābha-niścikīrṣā] — seeks robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites from others,
sbh1.3:11.30: and what is by non-Dharma is for him wrong livelihood.
sbh1.3:11.31: Thus that virtue is gripped by deficiency of livelihood.
sbh1.3:11.32: How is it fallen into the two extremes?
sbh1.3:11.33: When someone here is bent on the pleasure of sense-desires, supremely attached to them.
sbh1.3:11.34: He uses the robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — obtained either by Dharma or by non-Dharma —
sbh1.3:11.35: without seeing the danger, without knowing the escape. This is called one extreme.
sbh1.3:11.36: And again, here someone is bent on self-mortification; in manifold ways he scorches and torments himself.
sbh1.3:11.39: an ash-taker, one whose resort is the pestle,
sbh1.3:11.40: one whose resort is the plank,
sbh1.3:11.41: a squatter applied to the squatting-renunciation practice,
sbh1.3:11.43: up to three times [a day] he tends the fire; a water-immerser —
sbh1.3:11.44: up to three times [a day] he immerses in water;
sbh1.3:11.45: standing on one foot, he turns with the sun.
sbh1.3:11.46: Such, or any other such kind of application to self-mortification — this is called the second extreme.
sbh1.3:11.47: Thus it is fallen into the two extremes.
sbh1.3:11.48: How is it not leading out [aniḥsaraṇika]?
sbh1.3:11.49: When someone here clings to virtue or observance by [wrong] view:
sbh1.3:11.50: ‘By this very virtue or observance there will be purification,
sbh1.3:11.52: All the virtue of those outside [the Buddha’s dispensation] — even well-guarded, even well-purified — by such [a wrong-view] purification is called not-leading-out.
sbh1.3:11.54: How is it fallen from the undertaking?
sbh1.3:11.55: When someone here is wholly, entirely shameless, indifferent —
sbh1.3:11.57: of evil virtue, evil dharma, inwardly rotten, oozing, of impure-water-mixed-up nature,
sbh1.3:11.59: not a recluse but claiming to be a recluse, not a celibate but claiming to be celibate — thus it is fallen from the undertaking.
sbh1.3:11.60: By these ten causes virtue is ruined — this is called by the Blessed One the ruin of virtue.
sbh1.3:11.61: Moreover, the practice [of virtue] too was stated by the Blessed One.
sbh1.3:11.62: Now among these [ten] causes, [the ruin] is to be understood [especially] from two:
sbh1.3:11.63: namely, from not-leading-out and from falling-from-the-undertaking — and also from the other causes; [all] these are to be understood as the ruin of virtue.
sbh1.3:11.64: From these very causes set on the dark side, by their reverse — by the bright-side causes — the fullness of virtue is to be understood,
sbh1.3:11.66: In some places, again, the Blessed One speaks of virtue by the word ‘root.’
sbh1.3:11.67: As said: ‘He is one whose root is well-established, delighting in the calming of the mind,
sbh1.3:11.68: connected and disconnected from the seen-and-unseen, noble and evil’ — so the verse.
sbh1.3:12.1: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘ornament.’
sbh1.3:12.2: As stated: ‘A monk or nun endowed with the ornament of virtue abandons the unwholesome, cultivates the wholesome.’
sbh1.3:12.3: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘ointment.’
sbh1.3:12.5: ‘A monk or nun endowed with the ointment of virtue,’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:12.6: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘scent.’
sbh1.3:12.7: ‘There is that giving which is a kind of scent, whose scent reaches downwind, against the wind, [and] both with and against the wind.’
sbh1.3:12.8: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘good conduct’ [sucarita].
sbh1.3:12.10: ‘The fruit of good bodily conduct is to be desired in the visible-here-and-now and in the after-state; likewise of good verbal conduct.’
sbh1.3:12.11: In some places it is spoken of by the word ‘restraint.’
sbh1.3:12.13: ‘The giver, the donor, becomes endowed with virtue,
sbh1.3:12.14: established in restraint, of right view received, seeing the fruit.’
sbh1.3:12.17: restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa,’ [as elaborated above] in detail.
sbh1.3:12.18: For what reason did the Blessed One speak of virtue by the word ‘root’?
sbh1.3:12.19: Because the meaning of ‘root’ is the meaning of establishment, the meaning of basis.
sbh1.3:12.20: This very virtue is the establishment, the basis, for the arising and attainment of all worldly and supramundane pure, blameless, supreme, distinguished, pleasant-fruited dharmas; therefore it is spoken of by the word ‘root.’
sbh1.3:12.21: Just as the earth is the establishment, the basis, for the arising of grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees, just so [is] virtue, [as detailed] above.
sbh1.3:12.22: For what reason is virtue declared by the word ‘ornament’?
sbh1.3:12.24: Those other adornments — necklaces, bracelets, armlets, rings, garlands of gold and silver — only as long as one is young,
sbh1.3:12.25: youthful, with dark hair, possessing the freshness of youth, do those adornments, when put on him, [actually] adorn.
sbh1.3:12.26: But not so for one aged, old, weak, octogenarian or nonagenarian, broken-toothed, gray-haired — on such a one those adornments, put on, appear on the contrary as if mocking [him].
sbh1.3:12.27: In sickness, in loss of wealth, in loss of kin — when these befall — he does not shine [in such adornments].
sbh1.3:12.28: Virtue, however, is an adornment for all [people], at all times.
sbh1.3:12.29: Therefore it is spoken of by the word ‘ornament.’
sbh1.3:13.1: For what reason is virtue spoken of by the word ‘ointment’?
sbh1.3:13.2: Here, the great wholesome, blameless undertaking of virtue removes the bodily and mental burning caused by every undertaking of evil [contrary to] virtue —
sbh1.3:13.3: as for one scorched by heat in the great-summer-burning time, sandal ointment or camphor ointment [removes the burning]. For this reason virtue is spoken of by the word ‘ointment.’
sbh1.3:14.1: For what reason is virtue called ‘scent’?
sbh1.3:14.2: For a virtuous individual, in all directions and intermediate directions, fair fame, repute, voice, [and] eulogy go forth —
sbh1.3:14.3: just as, of various kinds of root-scents, sap-scents, or flower-scents, when wafted in the directions, an agreeable scent goes forth.
sbh1.3:14.4: For this reason virtue is spoken of by the word ‘scent.’
sbh1.3:15.1: For what reason is virtue called ‘good conduct’?
sbh1.3:15.2: ‘This conduct leads to ease, this conduct leads to heaven, leads to good destinies.’
sbh1.3:15.3: Therefore it is called good conduct.
sbh1.3:16.1: For what reason is virtue called ‘restraint’?
sbh1.3:16.2: This dharma has cessation [of unwholesome dharmas] as its own-nature, has the mark of cessation, has abstention as its own-nature.
sbh1.3:16.3: Therefore it is called by the word ‘restraint.’
sbh1.3:16.4: Of this restraint of virtue, the threefold review is the sign of purification.
sbh1.3:16.6: Namely: review of bodily action, review of verbal action, review of mental action.
sbh1.3:16.7: Reviewing these [three kinds of] action, he purifies the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:16.8: Whatever action he intends to perform with the body, that he reviews [thus]:
sbh1.3:16.9: ‘Is this bodily action of mine harmful, an affliction to others, unwholesome, leading to suffering, of painful result? Or is this bodily action of mine non-harmful — of myself and others — wholesome, leading to ease, of pleasant result?’ If, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this bodily action of mine is harmful, [either] of myself or of another, unwholesome, leading to suffering, of painful result,’ then, having so reviewed, he does not engage in it;
sbh1.3:16.10: that action he does not do,
sbh1.3:16.12: If, again, he knows: ‘this bodily action of mine is non-harmful, wholesome,’ [the rest] as before, that he does —
sbh1.3:16.13: that bodily action he does not withhold, but performs.
sbh1.3:16.14: Even an action that, taking up the past, has already been done by him through the body —
sbh1.3:16.16: ‘Was this [action] of mine harmful?’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:16.17: [He reviews it] with [the help of] wise co-religionists. If, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this action of mine is harmful,’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.18: in the presence of wise co-religionists he withholds,
sbh1.3:16.20: Even an action that, taking up the past, has already been done by him through the body —
sbh1.3:16.22: ‘Was this [action] of mine harmful?’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:16.23: [He reviews it] with [the help of] wise co-religionists. If, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this action of mine is harmful,’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.24: in the presence of wise co-religionists he confesses, [and] makes amends according to Dharma.
sbh1.3:16.25: If, on the other hand, reviewing thus, he knows: ‘this bodily action of mine is non-harmful,’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.26: by that very joy and gladness he dwells, day and night, much in training. Thus that bodily action of his is well reviewed
sbh1.3:16.28: namely, in past, future, and present times.
sbh1.3:16.29: As with bodily action, so verbal action is to be understood.
sbh1.3:16.30: Mind arises dependent on past formations;
sbh1.3:16.31: mind arises dependent on future and present formations.
sbh1.3:16.33: ‘Is this mind of mine harmful?’ [the rest] as before,
sbh1.3:16.34: up through: he does not produce [it];
sbh1.3:16.37: Conversely, on the bright side, he produces [it], does not withhold, [but] performs that mental action.
sbh1.3:16.38: Thus that mental action is by him reviewed
sbh1.3:16.40: namely, in past, future, and present times.
sbh1.3:16.41: For what reason? In past time, in future time, and in present time, whatever recluses or brahmins, having reviewed and purified bodily, verbal, and mental action, have lived extensively [in this way] — all of them have done so by such review and purification,
sbh1.3:16.42: as was said by the Blessed One concerning the Venerable Rāhula:
sbh1.3:16.43: ‘Bodily action, then verbal action, and also mental action, Rāhula —
sbh1.3:16.44: repeatedly review [them], remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.
sbh1.3:17.1: This is the work of the recluse — train in this, Rāhula.
sbh1.3:17.2: For one training therein, there is only good, not evil.’
sbh1.3:18.1: Here, that he investigates ‘bodily action, verbal action, mental action — is this harmful for me?’ [the rest] as before — this is the review.
sbh1.3:18.2: And that some [actions] he withholds and confesses, some he performs,
sbh1.3:18.3: and by that very joy and gladness — training day and night — he dwells much [in training] — this is called purification.
sbh1.3:18.4: Of the restraint of virtue thus purified, ten benefits are to be understood.
sbh1.3:18.6: [1] Here a virtuous one, free of regret, gains gladness; in a gladdened [mind] joy arises;
sbh1.3:18.7: with a joyful mind the body is tranquilized;
sbh1.3:18.8: with tranquilized body he feels pleasure;
sbh1.3:18.9: with pleased mind, the mind is concentrated;
sbh1.3:18.10: with concentrated mind he knows as it truly is,
sbh1.3:18.12: knowing-and-seeing as it truly is, he grows weary [of saṁsāra];
sbh1.3:18.13: wearied, he is detached [from passion]; detached, he is liberated; for one liberated, the knowing-and-seeing of liberation arises;
sbh1.3:18.14: [and so on] up through: he attains final nirvāṇa in the nirvāṇa-element without remainder.
sbh1.3:18.15: [Thus] a virtuous individual, by way of the purity of virtue, gains non-regret,
sbh1.3:18.16: and by gradual progression [proceeds] up to the going to nirvāṇa — this is the first benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:18.17: [2] Further, a virtuous individual, when the time of death is present, [reflects]: ‘good has been done by me, well [done]; good conduct of body, speech, [and] mind [has been done by me]; bad conduct of body [etc.] has not been done by me,’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:18.19: of those who have done merit, done wholesome deeds, done deeds [out of] fearfulness about evil — to that destiny shall I, after death, go.’ He gains this second [kind of] non-regret,
sbh1.3:18.20: [which leads] to a happy destiny. For a non-regretful individual, death is good,
sbh1.3:18.21: the time of death is good, the after-state is good.
sbh1.3:18.22: This is the second benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:19.1: [3] Further, of the virtuous individual, fair fame, repute, voice, [and] eulogy go forth.
sbh1.3:19.2: This is the third benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:20.1: [4] Further, the virtuous individual sleeps comfortably, dwells comfortably,
sbh1.3:20.2: with body and mind free from burning. This is the fourth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:20.3: [5] Further, the virtuous individual, even when asleep, is guarded by the deities.
sbh1.3:20.4: This is the fifth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:21.1: [6] Further, the virtuous individual is not suspicious,
sbh1.3:21.2: not afraid of [any] evil from outside, not of terrified mind.
sbh1.3:21.3: This is the sixth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:22.1: [7] Further, the virtuous individual — even when openings [for attack] are sought by killers [and] enemies — is guarded;
sbh1.3:22.2: knowing always ‘this individual is such [a virtuous one],’ they fall either into friendship with him or into a neutral disposition.
sbh1.3:22.3: This is the seventh benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:23.1: [8] Further, even when openings [for attack] are sought by [hostile] yakṣas of long standing or by amanuṣyas dwelling there, he is guarded —
sbh1.3:23.2: namely, by making that very virtue predominant.
sbh1.3:23.3: This is the eighth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:24.1: [9] Further, the virtuous individual, by Dharma [and] with little hardship, gains from others
sbh1.3:24.2: robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — that is, on account of the [further] addition of virtue, he is honored
sbh1.3:24.3: [and] esteemed by kings, royal ministers, townsmen, country-folk, the wealthy, the chiefs, [and] caravan leaders.
sbh1.3:24.4: This is the ninth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:25.1: [10] Further, [as] above, all his vows succeed.
sbh1.3:25.2: If he wishes, [saying]: ‘in the realm of desire — in the company of great kṣatriya-mahāsāla families, or great brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla families, or great householder-mahāsāla families, or among the deities of the four great kings, of the Trāyastriṁśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, [or] Paranirmitavaśavartin — may I be born in their company’ — [or] on account of the purity of virtue, the undertaking [of dispassion], the deep-rooted [skill], and entering the dhyānas, [‘may I] dwell at ease in the visible-here-and-now;
sbh1.3:25.3: and may I be born in the company of the form-realm deities and dwell [there]’ — this aspiration and vow of the virtuous, lust-free one succeeds.
sbh1.3:25.5: ‘[the eight] liberations [vimokṣa] may I attain and dwell [in them]’;
sbh1.3:25.6: or ‘in the company of the formless-realm deities may I be born,’ [the rest] as before.
sbh1.3:26.1: If he wishes, ‘may I attain final-cessation nirvāṇa,’ he attains [it].
sbh1.3:27.1: [This is] by the purity of that destiny of virtue, and [available] to the lust-free [individual] in all respects.
sbh1.3:27.2: This is to be understood as the tenth benefit of virtue.
sbh1.3:28.1: [Thus] the virtue-aggregate has been set forth by [its] division; the ruin and the fullness [of virtue] have been set forth;
sbh1.3:28.2: the synonyms have been set forth;
sbh1.3:28.3: the review constituting purification has been set forth, [and] the benefit has been set forth.
sbh1.3:29.1: This wholly complete restraint of virtue, [together with its] subsumed requisites, has been declared, set forth, opened up, [and] made manifest — wherein sons of good family, desirous of self-good and of asceticism and brahminhood [brāhmaṇya], should train.
sbh1.3:31.1: The division is to be known as threefold, the fullness as tenfold,
sbh1.3:31.2: the synonyms as six-fold; the purification is held as threefold,
sbh1.3:31.3: the benefit as tenfold — such is the restraint of virtue.
sbh1.3:32.1: What is restraint of the senses?
sbh1.3:32.2: When someone here dwells with guarded sense-doors, with mindfulness guarded, with alert mindfulness — [as elaborated in the standard formula].
sbh1.3:32.3: How does he dwell with guarded sense-doors, with mindfulness guarded?
sbh1.3:32.4: [And how] with alert mindfulness — [as elaborated] up through: he guards the mind-faculty by means of the mind-faculty.
sbh1.3:32.6: Thus he dwells with guarded sense-doors.
sbh1.3:32.7: How, then, is his mindfulness guarded?
sbh1.3:32.8: When someone here, taking the very [practice of] guarded sense-doors as predominant, holds firmly to what has been heard,
sbh1.3:32.10: And by that, he attains a mindfulness whose predominant ground is hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
sbh1.3:32.11: Of that mindfulness once attained — so that it is not forgotten, is firmly grasped, is not lost — he applies effort and practice, from time to time, on that same teaching he heard, and he applies effort and practice in reflecting on it and cultivating it.
sbh1.3:32.12: He does not let his application drop. Thus, of the mindfulness born from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the guarding is performed from time to time through the practice of those very three.
sbh1.3:32.13: Thus he becomes one of guarded mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.14: How does he have alert mindfulness?
sbh1.3:32.15: He becomes one constantly active in that very mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.17: Of these, *nityakāritā* (constant action) is what is called *sātatya-kāritā* (continual action).
sbh1.3:32.18: *Niryāṇa-kāritā* (action toward going-forth) is what is called *satkṛtya-kāritā* (action done with respect).
sbh1.3:32.19: He who acts thus — continually and with respect — is called one of alert mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.21: Thus he does not lose that mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.23: Thus in that very unlost mindfulness he attains the establishment of power.
sbh1.3:32.24: By which he becomes able and fit for the overcoming of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, dharmas.
sbh1.3:32.25: How is his mind guarded by mindfulness?
sbh1.3:32.26: Depending on the eye and forms, there arises
sbh1.3:32.27: eye-consciousness; immediately after eye-consciousness there arises
sbh1.3:32.28: discriminative mind-consciousness; by that discriminative mind-consciousness, one is drawn toward pleasing forms
sbh1.3:32.29: and turns away from displeasing forms.
sbh1.3:32.30: Taking [the discriminative mind-consciousness] itself as predominant, he guards [the mind] against the unwise discrimination that produces defilement,
sbh1.3:32.31: so that defilement does not arise.
sbh1.3:32.32: Likewise, depending on ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind together with their respective objects, mind-consciousness arises.
sbh1.3:32.33: And that mind-consciousness, accompanied by unwise discrimination, produces defilement,
sbh1.3:32.34: by which one is drawn toward pleasing dharmas
sbh1.3:32.35: and turns away from displeasing dharmas.
sbh1.3:32.36: He guards that mental state against the unwise discrimination that produces defilement — and thus defilement does not arise in him.
sbh1.3:32.37: Thus he becomes one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness.
sbh1.3:32.38: How is he one who maintains a balanced state?
sbh1.3:32.41: Having guarded that mental state from the unwise discrimination that produces defilement, he settles it in wholesome equanimity or in indeterminate equanimity.
sbh1.3:32.42: Therefore he is called one who maintains a balanced state.
sbh1.3:32.43: Thus he becomes one who maintains a balanced state.
sbh1.3:32.44: And how, again, does he guard the mental state from the unwise discrimination that produces defilement?
sbh1.3:32.45: He does not become a seizer of signs.
sbh1.3:32.46: In those forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas he does not become a seizer of secondary features — that on account of which evil unwholesome dharmas would flow into his mind.
sbh1.3:32.47: If, even so, through lapse of mindfulness or through the strength of his defilements, sign-seizing or secondary-feature-seizing arises despite his avoidance,
sbh1.3:32.48: and the evil unwholesome dharmas — ill-grasped — indeed follow upon them,
sbh1.3:32.49: he then applies the mind to their restraint.
sbh1.3:32.50: By these two modes, the mental state is guarded from the unwise discrimination that produces defilement.
sbh1.3:33.1: And how, having guarded the mental state by these two modes, does he settle it in wholesome or indeterminate equanimity?
sbh1.3:33.4: As [the standard formula] says: ‘he guards the eye-faculty, attains restraint by the eye-faculty,’
sbh1.3:33.5: and just as ‘he guards the eye-faculty, attains restraint by the eye-faculty,’
sbh1.3:33.6: so for the ear, nose, tongue, and body — and he guards the mind-faculty, attains restraint by the mind-faculty.
sbh1.3:33.7: By these two modes, he settles that mental state in wholesome or indeterminate equanimity.
sbh1.3:34.1: How, with respect to the forms cognizable by the eye, does he not become a seizer of signs?
sbh1.3:34.3: of the form which is the range of eye-consciousness, becoming a seizer of that range
sbh1.3:34.5: That is what it means to become a seizer of signs.
sbh1.3:34.6: Namely, in forms cognizable by the eye — and in forms cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — there is another order of [object], the sign.
sbh1.3:34.7: If, then, he avoids that range —
sbh1.3:34.8: [the range] of eye-consciousness too — he does not become a seizer of signs
sbh1.3:34.9: in forms cognizable by the eye, and likewise in dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness.
sbh1.3:34.10: How does he not become a seizer of secondary features?
sbh1.3:34.11: [That is, with respect to] forms cognizable by the eye.
sbh1.3:34.13: in those very forms cognizable by the eye, the range of the discriminative mind-consciousness that arises immediately along with eye-consciousness — when [that range tends] toward lust, toward hatred, or toward delusion — he avoids that range,
sbh1.3:34.15: for that mind-consciousness — and thus he does not become a seizer of secondary features
sbh1.3:34.16: in forms cognizable by the eye,
sbh1.3:34.17: or in dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — the other order of sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing.
sbh1.3:34.18: Concretely: sign-seizing is when, having brought to presence the mental engagement born of it, he sees with the eye the forms that have come into manifestation.
sbh1.3:34.19: And the seizing of secondary features [proceeds as follows]:
sbh1.3:34.20: [having] those same forms that have come into eye-manifestation, having brought to presence the mental engagement born of them, he sees them,
sbh1.3:34.21: but further, hears about them from another in a follow-up way:
sbh1.3:34.22: ‘Such are these forms — these eye-cognizable forms’ — and the names, words, and letters that follow upon those [reports], making them predominant, relying on them, established in them, this person discriminates the eye-cognizable forms in accord with what he has heard. This is called
sbh1.3:34.24: As with eye-cognizable forms, so it is to be understood with dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, mind.
sbh1.3:34.25: Such sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing — when there is some [form] on account of which, with respect to which, and by means of which as the predominant condition, his evil unwholesome dharmas flow into his mind:
sbh1.3:34.26: where there is such a cause, such an occasion, such a predominant condition for evil unwholesome dharmas to flow into the mind,
sbh1.3:34.27: the sign-seizing, the secondary-feature-seizing, the unwise seizing — that which is the cause, the occasion, the predominant condition for his evil unwholesome dharmas to flow into the mind:
sbh1.3:34.28: that very form of sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing he avoids.
sbh1.3:34.30: Lust, and the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct produced by lust;
sbh1.3:34.32: and the bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct produced by [hatred and] delusion — these are called evil unwholesome dharmas.
sbh1.3:34.33: How do they ‘flow into the mind’?
sbh1.3:34.36: Associated with that object-support of mind-consciousness, the bodily-, verbal-, and mental-misconduct-producing lust, hatred, and delusion arise, go, follow along.
sbh1.3:34.37: Therefore they are said to ‘flow into the mind.’
sbh1.3:35.1: Thus, the defilement that would arise — through sign-seizing or secondary-feature-seizing — in eye-cognizable forms (and so on up to mind-cognizable dharmas) does not arise for one who avoids sign-seizing and secondary-feature-seizing.
sbh1.3:35.2: If, even so, through lapse of mindfulness or through the strength of his defilements, evil unwholesome dharmas arise even while he is dwelling alone — taking previously seen eye-cognizable forms as predominant, or taking previously experienced dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as predominant — once they have arisen he does not accommodate them: he abandons them, purifies them, puts an end to them.
sbh1.3:35.3: Therefore he is said to apply himself to their restraint.
sbh1.3:35.4: On forms toward which the eye is [properly] to be directed,
sbh1.3:35.5: and on dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind toward which the mind is [properly] to be directed,
sbh1.3:35.7: in such a way that he is not defiled.
sbh1.3:35.8: Thus the mind-faculty is guarded by him from that defilement.
sbh1.3:35.9: Therefore it is said: ‘he guards the mind-faculty.’
sbh1.3:35.10: On forms cognizable by the eye toward which the eye-faculty is not to be directed,
sbh1.3:35.11: and on dharmas cognizable by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind toward which the mind-faculty is not to be directed —
sbh1.3:35.12: to those he does not direct [his faculties] at all, in any way.
sbh1.3:35.13: Therefore it is said: ‘he attains restraint by the eye-faculty,’
sbh1.3:35.14: and so on up through ‘he attains restraint by the mind-faculty.’
sbh1.3:35.15: This much is the detailed exposition of sense-restraint, to be understood.
sbh1.3:35.17: by what one restrains, from what one restrains, how one restrains, and what the restraint itself is —
sbh1.3:35.18: all this gathered into one is called restraint of the senses.
sbh1.3:35.20: By guarded mindfulness — by that he restrains.
sbh1.3:35.23: he restrains the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-faculty.
sbh1.3:35.26: From pleasing- and displeasing-form forms, sounds, and so on up to dharmas — from these he restrains.
sbh1.3:35.28: He does not become a seizer of signs, does not become a seizer of secondary features — that on account of which evil unwholesome [dharmas would arise]; he attains restraint [from them].
sbh1.3:35.30: And what is the restraint itself?
sbh1.3:35.31: That by which he is one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness,
sbh1.3:35.32: and one who maintains a balanced state —
sbh1.3:35.36: the object to be restrained, and the restraint itself —
sbh1.3:35.37: these gathered into one are called restraint of the senses.
sbh1.3:35.38: What is the means of restraint?
sbh1.3:35.39: What is meant by [the standard formula]: ‘he becomes one of guarded mindfulness, alert mindfulness; seeing forms with the eye, he does not become a seizer of signs, does not become a seizer of secondary features — up through: cognizing dharmas with the mind, he does not become a seizer of signs, does not become a seizer of secondary features’ —
sbh1.3:35.40: ‘that on account of which evil unwholesome dharmas would flow into the mind,
sbh1.3:35.41: to their restraint he applies himself;
sbh1.3:35.42: he guards the faculty, attains restraint by the faculty.’
sbh1.3:35.43: This is called the means of restraint.
sbh1.3:35.44: What is the object to be restrained?
sbh1.3:35.45: Eye-and-form, and so on up through mind-and-dharmas — this is called the object to be restrained.
sbh1.3:35.46: And what is the restraint itself?
sbh1.3:35.48: ‘he is one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness,
sbh1.3:35.49: one who maintains a balanced state’ — this is called restraint.
sbh1.3:35.50: This restraint of the senses is, in brief, of two kinds:
sbh1.3:35.51: that grounded in the power of reflective discrimination (*pratisaṁkhyāna-bala*), and that grounded in the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).
sbh1.3:35.52: Of these, the one grounded in the power of reflective discrimination is that by which he sees danger in the sense-objects,
sbh1.3:35.53: but does not yet remove that danger,
sbh1.3:35.55: The one grounded in the power of cultivation is that by which he sees danger in the sense-objects and also removes that danger,
sbh1.3:35.57: By sense-restraint grounded in the power of reflective discrimination, the obsession of defilement that takes sense-objects as its object-support does not arise, does not come to manifest —
sbh1.3:35.58: but he does not yet abandon, does not yet eradicate, the latent tendency settled in the [karmic] basis.
sbh1.3:35.59: By sense-restraint grounded in the power of cultivation, that same obsession of defilement does not arise, does not come to manifest —
sbh1.3:35.60: and at all times he also abandons the latent tendency settled in the [karmic] basis,
sbh1.3:35.62: This is the distinction; this is the import.
sbh1.3:35.63: This [non-arising and non-manifestation of defilement] is the [shared] negative work of both kinds of sense-restraint — that grounded in reflective discrimination and that grounded in cultivation.
sbh1.3:35.64: The sense-restraint grounded in the power of reflective discrimination belongs to the path of requisites (*saṁbhāra-mārga*).
sbh1.3:35.65: The sense-restraint grounded in the power of cultivation,
sbh1.3:35.66: by contrast, is to be understood as falling within the dispassion-stage proper.
sbh1.3:36.1: What is knowing the right measure in food?
sbh1.3:36.2: When someone here takes food with [proper] reflection —
sbh1.3:36.3: not for arrogance, not for adornment, not for embellishment, [as elaborated in the standard formula] above.
sbh1.3:36.4: How does he take food with [proper] reflection?
sbh1.3:36.5: ‘Reflection’ here refers to that wisdom by which he sees the danger in solid food, and seeing the danger, having grasped the fault — and grasping the fault — he eats.
sbh1.3:37.2: [It is the danger seen] in that very solid food by way of the consequence of consumption, the consequence of transformation, or the consequence of seeking.
sbh1.3:37.3: What is the consumption-consequence danger [in food]?
sbh1.3:37.4: When someone here, at the time of taking food endowed with color, endowed with smell, endowed with taste, very fine —
sbh1.3:37.5: of that food just put into the mouth, ground by the apparatus of the teeth, made wet by the flowing of saliva,
sbh1.3:37.7: at the time when it has rolled down through the throat-tube,
sbh1.3:37.8: that former, original agreeableness, the agreeable taste — that he wholly, entirely abandons,
sbh1.3:37.10: and in that transformation underway, it appears like vomit.
sbh1.3:37.11: And [as for] that very state — if the consumer-individual were to attend to its appearance, to recollect it, his desire to enjoy [it] would in no way remain, [not] even with respect to [as-yet] untransformed, fine food.
sbh1.3:37.12: What more is to be said of that [later] state? By these manifold modes, by this sequence, with food-consumption as the predominant [factor], this beautiful color is altered, and danger appears, [the food] coming under [the category of] the foul.
sbh1.3:37.16: What is the transformation-consequence danger in food?
sbh1.3:37.17: When he has taken that food and is satisfied, [and] when it undergoes transformation — in the middle watch of the night or in the last watch — it then generates and increases blood, flesh, sinew, bone, skin, and many other [tissues],
sbh1.3:37.18: [as well as] impure substances in this body.
sbh1.3:37.20: having undergone further transformation, it descends to the lower [part of the body],
sbh1.3:37.21: [the elimination of] which during the day must be attended to with distaste.
sbh1.3:37.22: And what is touched by him [in this elimination] —
sbh1.3:37.23: the hand or the foot, or some other limb or sub-limb — has thereafter to be hidden from outsiders, guarded both from himself and from others.
sbh1.3:37.24: And on that account [of food] arise
sbh1.3:37.25: in his body many bodily afflictions,
sbh1.3:37.26: namely: tumor, boil, eczema, itching, leprosy, skin-disease, pallor-disease, fever, cough, swelling, consumption, epilepsy, intestinal infection, jaundice, [disease of the] blood, [and] bile-fistula — these and other such bodily afflictions arise in the body.
sbh1.3:37.27: Or what was eaten goes bad,
sbh1.3:37.28: on account of which cholera appears in his body.
sbh1.3:37.29: This is called the danger of transformation, namely, in food.
sbh1.3:37.30: What, then, is the seeking-consequence danger in food?
sbh1.3:37.31: The seeking-consequence danger is of many kinds: caused by gathering,
sbh1.3:37.35: caused by lack of independence, and caused by misconduct.
sbh1.3:37.36: What is the danger in food

sbh1.3:37.60: [strike each other] with clod, with stick, with weapon. This is called the danger caused by loss of affection.

sbh1.3:38.1: with raging elephant, with chariot, with foot-soldier they engage.

sbh1.3:38.3: or mere [the prospect of] death is suffering. This is called
sbh1.3:38.4: the danger caused by insatiability — or whatever else is of such kind.

sbh1.3:39.7: This is called the danger caused by lack of independence — or whatever else is of such kind.
sbh1.3:39.8: What is the danger caused by misconduct?

sbh1.3:39.16: and dying in such an [evil] manner, he is reborn in the lower realms —
sbh1.3:39.17: namely in the hells, the animal-realm, [or] the ghost-realm.
sbh1.3:39.18: This is called the danger caused by misconduct.
sbh1.3:39.20: ‘This food, in its seeking, is dangerous;

sbh1.3:39.29: Those who are practiced merely [at the level of] body-maintenance are not well-practiced; those who are content with merely [the level of] body-sustaining in the body are not [truly] content [in the noble sense]; they experience neither the full, blameless benefit of food.
sbh1.3:39.30: Those who, on the other hand, are not [merely] content with body-sustaining — they are not [merely] so-practiced [but] well-practiced; rather, depending on that very body-sustaining, they are practiced for the perfection of the holy life — [they are] well-practiced, and they [do] experience the full, blameless benefit.
sbh1.3:39.31: ‘How would it be like me, were I to dwell content with the slight, lower-grade benefit-portion of food alone?
sbh1.3:39.32: It would not be fitting for me to fall into the company of fools, into Dharma-companionship with fools.’ Having thus known the wholly complete danger in food, with [proper] reflection he becomes a seer of danger and seeker of escape — for the sake of escape from food alone. It occurs to him:
sbh1.3:39.33: ‘These donor-patrons, having gathered their enjoyments with difficulty, undergoing great seeking-caused danger, hard-pressing themselves, give us [the produce of] their skin-and-flesh and blood.
sbh1.3:39.34: These [patrons], out of compassion, [are] desirous of the distinguished fruit. As for this alms-food so attained by us, the fitting form of enjoyment would be this: that I, having attained [it],
sbh1.3:39.35: should place myself in self-restraint and enjoy [it] in such a way that those services rendered by them might bear great fruit, great benefit, great glory, [and] great extension; and that, like the moon, I should approach their families — withdrawn in body, withdrawn in mind, possessed of moral shame, non-brazen, non-self-aggrandizing, non-deprecating-of-others, with mind well-clear and glad at one’s own gain, and equally with clear and glad mind at another’s gain — and with such [a] mind would I again approach their families.
sbh1.3:39.36: How is this to be obtained by one gone forth [into the homeless life], [going] in others’ families? — [thinking,] ‘let others give me food’ —
sbh1.3:39.37: honoringly, not without honor; plentifully, not scantily; finely, not crudely; swiftly, not slowly; properly.
sbh1.3:39.38: [I should resolve:] walking thus, approaching families, if others do not give, on their account I should not sully myself with a mind of resentment or a mind of hostility,
sbh1.3:39.39: and further, on that account, with the breaking up of the body, I should not encounter the dejection of rebirth in the lower realms —
sbh1.3:39.40: namely, by taking that very mind-of-resentment, mind-of-hostility as predominant. [And if] they give without honor, not with honor — scantily, not plentifully —
sbh1.3:39.41: crudely, not finely; slowly, not swiftly —
sbh1.3:39.42: [I should not] on that account sully myself with a mind of resentment and hostility,’ [the rest] as elaborated above.

sbh1.3:40.120: Such being the case, all these terms become explanatory of balanced-acting in food.
sbh1.3:40.121: This is called knowing the right measure in food,
sbh1.3:42.1: What is application to wakefulness in the early and late watches of the night?
sbh1.3:42.6: Here [the early watch is] this evening-time, midnight, [or] evening — taking up [the period] from the sun’s setting, the first part of the night, the somewhat-more-than-a-watch portion.
sbh1.3:42.8: [the text describes it] when it says:
sbh1.3:42.9: ‘by day, by walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas;
sbh1.3:42.10: having purified [the mind], washing his feet outside the dwelling, entering the dwelling, he lies down on the right side,
sbh1.3:42.11: foot placed on foot, perceiving light, mindful,
sbh1.3:42.12: fully aware, attending to the perception of rising; in the last watch of the night, rising lightly, very lightly, by walking and sitting he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.’
sbh1.3:42.13: This is the application of the wakefulness-yoga.
sbh1.3:42.14: When [the practitioner] hears of the wakefulness-yoga of the Blessed Buddha’s disciples,
sbh1.3:42.15: he there becomes desirous of training:
sbh1.3:42.16: ‘Just as it [really] is, taking up this wakefulness-yoga authorized by the Buddhas, I shall accomplish the application to wakefulness’ — that desire, [that] energy,
sbh1.3:42.20: [and] undertaking [samādāna] — [all these are] blameless [marks of right effort].
sbh1.3:42.21: How, by walking and sitting, does he purify the mind of obscuring dharmas?
sbh1.3:42.23: is taken [as the period] from the sun’s rising up to its setting. ‘Walking’ —
sbh1.3:42.25: back-and-forth movement on a wide, prepared piece of ground,
sbh1.3:42.27: is when someone here sits on a couch, on a stool, on a grass-mat,
sbh1.3:42.29: having set the body upright, establishing mindfulness facing forward.
sbh1.3:42.31: Obscuring dharmas are those that stand in [the same] place as the hindrances. What other obscuration-place dharmas [are there]? Sense-desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, doubt; the perception of the not-foul, the sign of resistance, [mental] darkness, recollection of kin, country, [or] recreation, past laughter, play, sound, gatherings; and [unwise reflection on] the three times —
sbh1.3:42.32: [that is,] unwise dharma-reflection that pertains to the three times.
sbh1.3:42.33: From these, how, by walking, does he purify the mind?
sbh1.3:42.34: [And] from how many [does he so purify it]?
sbh1.3:42.35: From sloth-and-torpor and from the [other] obscuration that is the food of sloth-and-torpor he purifies [the mind].
sbh1.3:42.36: The light-sign [āloka-saṁjñā] is by him well, thoroughly grasped,
sbh1.3:42.39: He, with mind accompanied by light, accompanied by radiance — under cover or in the open, while walking on the walking-path — by some clarifying object brightens the mind,
sbh1.3:42.42: namely, by recollection of the Buddha, [recollection of the] Dharma, [the] Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, [and the] deities.
sbh1.3:42.43: Or [he draws on] those dharmas which he has heard, grasped, [and] retained that concern the danger of sloth-and-torpor —
sbh1.3:42.44: namely, [from the twelve aṅgas:] sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhuta-dharma, [and] upadeśa — wherein, in many ways, sloth-and-torpor is censured and deplored,
sbh1.3:42.47: Those [passages], in detail, he recites with his voice,
sbh1.3:42.48: or he proclaims them to others, or reflects on their meaning,
sbh1.3:42.49: weighs them, examines them; or he gazes around at the directions,
sbh1.3:42.50: or fixes his gaze on the four constellations of stars and planets, [or] moistens the face with water.
sbh1.3:42.51: Thus his obsession by sloth-and-torpor, when unarisen, does not arise; and when arisen, departs. Thus by him the mind is purified of that obscuring dharma.
sbh1.3:42.52: By sitting, from which obscuring dharmas does he purify the mind?
sbh1.3:42.53: From sense-desire, ill-will, restlessness-and-regret, doubt, and the [other] dharmas that feed them.
sbh1.3:42.54: When the obsession of sense-desire has arisen, for its dispelling — or when it has not arisen, for its remoteness — sitting cross-legged, having set the body upright, having established mindfulness facing forward, he attends to the dark-livid, the festering, the worm-eaten, the swollen, the chewed, the bloody, the bone, the skeleton, or some other excellent sign of concentration;
sbh1.3:42.55: or [he draws on] those dharmas which, [touching on] the abandonment of sense-lust itself, have been grasped for the abandonment of sense-lust,
sbh1.3:42.56: retained, mastered by voice, examined by mind, well penetrated by view — namely sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, [as elaborated] above:
sbh1.3:42.57: those [passages] which in many ways censure and depreciate sense-lust, sense-desire, sense-attachment, sense-restraint, sense-fixation,
sbh1.3:42.59: and praise the abandonment of sense-lust in many ways,
sbh1.3:42.61: To those very dharmas — sitting thus — he attends wisely; thus his unarisen sense-desire-obsession does not arise,
sbh1.3:42.63: Now in [the case of] ill-will, this is the distinction:
sbh1.3:42.64: sitting thus, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness — free of enmity, free of opposition, free of harm, vast, become great, boundless, well cultivated — resolving on one direction, having brought it to mind, having attained [the state], he dwells;
sbh1.3:42.65: so a second, so a third, so a fourth [direction] — upward, downward, across — [pervading] the entire boundless world. In the [case of the] hindrance of doubt, the distinction is:
sbh1.3:42.67: to the past he does not unwisely attend,
sbh1.3:42.68: to the future and the present he does not unwisely attend [in such manner as]:
sbh1.3:42.69: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past?
sbh1.3:42.70: Or who was I in the past?
sbh1.3:42.71: How was I in the past?
sbh1.3:42.73: in the future? How shall I be in the future? Being what shall I be?
sbh1.3:42.74: From where has this being come?
sbh1.3:42.75: Falling from here, whither shall he go?’
sbh1.3:42.76: Having avoided such unwise attention, he attends wisely [to]
sbh1.3:42.80: the real as real, the unreal as unreal —
sbh1.3:42.81: only cause, only effect; he does not superimpose what does not exist,
sbh1.3:42.82: [and] does not destroy what does exist, does not depreciate [it].
sbh1.3:42.83: He knows the real as real,
sbh1.3:42.84: namely as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self — [seeing] impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self dharmas [as such]. He, thus wisely attending, is without doubt and without indecision about the Buddha,
sbh1.3:42.85: [without doubt] about the Dharma, the Saṅgha, suffering, origin, cessation, path, cause, [and] about dependently-originated dharmas — without doubt,
sbh1.3:42.87: The rest [is to be understood] as above.
sbh1.3:42.88: Now, regarding ill-will, it should be said:
sbh1.3:42.89: the [counter-]dharmas grasped by him with respect to resistance and the resistance-sign, [and grasped] for its abandonment, [as detailed] above;
sbh1.3:42.90: regarding restlessness-and-regret, it should be said:
sbh1.3:42.91: the [counter-]dharmas grasped, with respect to restlessness-and-regret, [and grasped] for its abandonment, [as elaborated] above;
sbh1.3:42.92: regarding doubt, it should be said:
sbh1.3:42.93: those [counter-]dharmas grasped by him with respect to doubt, [and grasped] for its abandonment, [as elaborated] above. By this [practice], the mind is purified of the sense-desire-hindrance, [and] of the ill-will-, sloth-and-torpor-, restlessness-and-regret-, [and] doubt-hindrances,
sbh1.3:42.94: and of the obscuring dharmas that are their food. Therefore he says: ‘by walking and sitting he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.’
sbh1.3:42.95: And this is the dharma-predominant [purification of mind from obscuring dharmas].
sbh1.3:42.96: There is also the self-predominant and world-predominant purification of mind from obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.98: When, on the arising of some particular hindrance, recognizing its unsuitability for oneself, he does not accommodate the arisen hindrance —
sbh1.3:42.99: he abandons, dispels, puts an end to [it, thinking]:
sbh1.3:42.100: ‘Let me not be known on account of that hindrance as a maker of mental corruption, a maker of wisdom-weakness, [as one] on the side of dejection.’ Thus, making the self predominant, he purifies the mind from the obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.101: How, making the world predominant, does he purify the mind from obscuring dharmas?
sbh1.3:42.102: Here, when a hindrance has arisen for him, or its time of arising is present,
sbh1.3:42.103: it occurs to him: ‘If I should produce an unarisen hindrance, the Teacher would reproach me, and the deities, the wise, [and] my co-religionists would censure me, regarding [it] as non-Dharma.’
sbh1.3:42.104: [Thus,] making the world predominant, he purifies the mind from the obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.105: Here, when a hindrance has arisen for him, or its time of arising is present, it occurs to him: ‘If I should produce an unarisen hindrance,
sbh1.3:42.106: the Teacher would reproach me, and the deities,
sbh1.3:42.107: the wise, [and] my co-religionists would censure me, regarding [it] as non-Dharma.’
sbh1.3:42.108: He, making the world predominant, both does not produce the unarisen hindrance, and, for the protection of the arisen abode [in practice] — namely, [conforming to] world-conduct — will follow accordingly. [In this way,] in the first watch of the night, by walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.109: Having purified the mind of obscuring dharmas, washing his feet outside the dwelling,
sbh1.3:42.110: [and] having washed, entering the dwelling, he lies down —
sbh1.3:42.111: only for the [re-]invigoration of his own native great elements [dhātu], [thinking]:
sbh1.3:42.112: ‘This body, when [thus] replenished, will be more workable
sbh1.3:42.113: and more amenable in the continuous, one-sided application to the wholesome.’
sbh1.3:42.114: For what reason does he lie down on [his right] side?
sbh1.3:42.117: The lion, among all animals of the animal-womb, is the boldest, the most enthusiastic, of firm valor.
sbh1.3:42.118: The monk too, applied to wakefulness, with aroused energy, dwells
sbh1.3:42.120: Hence for him the lion-couch is appropriate — not the ghost-couch, the deity-couch, nor the sense-pleasure-enjoyer’s couch —
sbh1.3:42.121: for they [whose couches those are] are all indolent, of low vigor, of slow strength and valor.
sbh1.3:42.122: Moreover, this is dharma-nature: for one who lies down on the right side in lion-fashion, there is not such scattering of the limbs,
sbh1.3:42.123: no forgetfulness of mindfulness for one [thus] sleeping,
sbh1.3:42.124: and he does not sleep deeply,
sbh1.3:42.125: and he does not see evil dreams.
sbh1.3:42.126: For one who lies down otherwise, the contrary faults are to be understood.
sbh1.3:42.127: Therefore he says: ‘he lies down on the right side.’
sbh1.3:42.128: The light-sign is by him well grasped,
sbh1.3:42.131: Just attending to it, with mind accompanied by light, he lies down,
sbh1.3:42.132: and for him, even sleeping, the mind does not enter a
sbh1.3:42.133: darkened state. Thus, perceiving light, he lies down.
sbh1.3:42.134: How, mindful, does he lie down?
sbh1.3:42.136: reflected on, cultivated, wholesome, connected with meaning — their consequence is mindfulness, [continuing] up to the time of sleep,
sbh1.3:42.137: such that, even while he sleeps, those very dharmas speak to him as if [he were] awake, and the mind moves abundantly in those very dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.138: Thus, as it were by mindfulness, with mindfulness,
sbh1.3:42.139: with wholesome mind, he lies down —
sbh1.3:42.142: How, fully aware, does he lie down?
sbh1.3:42.143: For him, sleeping thus mindfully, when at any time, by some secondary defilement, mental defilement occurs,
sbh1.3:42.144: of that arising defilement he is rightly fully aware; he does not accommodate, he abandons, he penetrates [it],
sbh1.3:42.145: he turns the mind back [from it].
sbh1.3:42.146: Therefore he is said to lie down fully aware.
sbh1.3:42.147: How, attending to the perception of rising, does he lie down?
sbh1.3:42.148: He lies down having made the mind held [steady] by energy,
sbh1.3:42.149: with well-awakening, well-uplifted, well-gladdened mind, just like a forest deer;
sbh1.3:42.150: he does not, completely, entirely, leave the mind plunged in [sloth],
sbh1.3:42.154: ‘Oh, may I in every respect, in every way, accomplish the wakefulness authorized by the Buddhas!’
sbh1.3:42.155: And for its accomplishment he dwells with hope, with relish, with application, with desire, and is intensely yoked.
sbh1.3:42.157: ‘Just as today, for the sake of wakefulness with aroused energy, I have dwelt — and, for the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, skilled, non-lazy, endowed with [the capacity for] rising — tomorrow at dawn, when night has gone forth, in still greater measure I shall dwell with aroused energy, endowed with [the capacity for] rising.’
sbh1.3:42.158: Now, by [the first kind of] rising-perception he [avoids] sleeping deeply,
sbh1.3:42.159: by which he is able, lightly very lightly at rising-time, to rise — not waking after the time has passed.
sbh1.3:42.160: By the second [kind of] rising-perception, he arranges the lion-couch authorized by the Buddhas, neither subtracting nor adding [from it].
sbh1.3:42.161: By the third [kind of] rising-perception, the desire [for wakefulness-yoga] he does not let slacken.
sbh1.3:42.162: When forgetfulness arises, in each subsequent moment he applies himself to renewed undertaking.
sbh1.3:42.163: Thus, attending to the rising-perception, he lies down.
sbh1.3:42.164: He, in the last watch of the night, lightly very lightly waking, purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.166: is [also] said to be the late-night, somewhat-more-than-a-watch portion.
sbh1.3:42.168: fully aware, attending to the perception of rising, having let the middle watch — [also] somewhat-more-than-a-watch — pass in torpor, in [proper] time he rises up.
sbh1.3:42.169: [Thus] at that time he rises up,
sbh1.3:42.171: Having risen, not overcome by strong sloth-and-torpor obsession,
sbh1.3:42.172: by which there would be in his rising slowness, sluggishness, [or] laziness and indolence;
sbh1.3:42.173: rather, in the absence of that slowness, sluggishness, laziness and indolence, his rising is lightly, very lightly, by mere effort, without [internal] battle. The purification from the obscuring dharmas is to be understood as above.
sbh1.3:42.174: This much is the detailed division of application to wakefulness in the early and late watches of the night.
sbh1.3:42.176: Here, for the person applied to wakefulness-yoga, there are four right tasks.
sbh1.3:42.178: [1] As long as he is awake, he does not let go of the wholesome side,
sbh1.3:42.179: [remaining] in continuous, one-sided cultivation of wholesome dharmas; [2] and at the [proper] time he lies down,
sbh1.3:42.181: [3] and while sleeping, with mind undefiled he lets torpor descend,
sbh1.3:42.183: [4] and at the [proper] time he wakes,
sbh1.3:42.185: Taking up these four right tasks, the application to wakefulness has been taught by the Blessed One to the disciples.
sbh1.3:42.188: ‘by day, by walking and sitting, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas;
sbh1.3:42.189: thus in the first watch of the night,’ by this the first right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.190: namely: as long as he is awake, he does not let go of the wholesome side,
sbh1.3:42.191: [remaining] in continuous, one-sided cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
sbh1.3:42.193: ‘washing the feet outside the dwelling, entering the dwelling, he lies down on the right side,
sbh1.3:42.194: foot placed on foot,’ by this the second right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.195: namely: at the [proper] time he lies down,
sbh1.3:42.199: fully aware, attending to the perception of rising, he lies down,’ by this the third right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.200: namely: with mind undefiled he lets torpor descend,
sbh1.3:42.202: When he then says: ‘in the last watch of the night, lightly very lightly waking, he purifies the mind of obscuring dharmas,’ by this the fourth right task is declared,
sbh1.3:42.203: namely: at the [proper] time he wakes,
sbh1.3:42.205: Thus where it is said ‘perceiving light, mindful, fully aware, attending to the rising-perception, he lies down,’
sbh1.3:42.206: from [these] two causes, with mind undefiled he lets torpor descend —
sbh1.3:42.207: namely, by mindfulness and full awareness; [and] from two further causes he wakes in time,
sbh1.3:42.209: namely, by perception of light and perception of rising.
sbh1.3:42.210: How, again, having grasped a wholesome object-support, does he [go to] sleep?
sbh1.3:42.211: By full awareness, [namely] that, when his mind has fallen away from the wholesome object [and] become defiled, he rightly knows [this] lightly very lightly.
sbh1.3:42.212: Thus by these two causes his sleep is undefiled.
sbh1.3:42.213: And by perception of light and perception of rising,
sbh1.3:42.215: [and] his torpor-obsession does not become far-going.
sbh1.3:42.216: Thus by these two causes he wakes in time,
sbh1.3:42.218: [Next:] dwelling with full awareness [saṁprajāna-vihāritā]. What is it?
sbh1.3:42.219: When someone here dwells with full awareness in setting forth and returning,
sbh1.3:42.220: in looking ahead and looking around, in bending and stretching [the limbs], in wearing the saṅghāṭi-robe and [carrying the] bowl,
sbh1.3:42.221: in eating, drinking, chewing, tasting, in sitting, lying, [and] waking, in speaking, in silence, in the dispelling of sleep-fatigue — he dwells with full awareness.
sbh1.3:42.224: What is dwelling with full awareness in setting forth and returning?
sbh1.3:42.226: when someone here approaches a village
sbh1.3:42.227: or another village, a family or another family, a dwelling or another dwelling.
sbh1.3:42.229: when someone here returns from another village or from a village,
sbh1.3:42.230: from another village, from a family, from another family, from a dwelling, from another dwelling.
sbh1.3:42.231: [Now,] dwelling with full awareness [in setting forth and returning]:
sbh1.3:43.1: Setting forth, he rightly knows ‘I am setting forth’;
sbh1.3:43.3: here I should not set forth’ —
sbh1.3:43.5: ‘this is for me a time of approach, this is not a time of approach’ —
sbh1.3:43.7: This is called for him full awareness.
sbh1.3:43.8: He, endowed with that full awareness,
sbh1.3:43.9: setting forth, knows ‘I am setting forth’;
sbh1.3:43.12: and at the [proper] time he sets forth, not out of time,
sbh1.3:43.14: with such conduct, with such deportment, he sets forth. This is called for him dwelling with full awareness, namely in setting forth and returning.
sbh1.3:43.15: What is looking ahead, what is looking around?
sbh1.3:43.16: What is dwelling with full awareness in looking ahead and looking around?
sbh1.3:43.17: For him, [while engaged] in the previously proclaimed dharmas of setting forth and returning, that seeing of forms with the eye which, without prior thought, without prior desire,
sbh1.3:43.18: occurs in between — this is called looking ahead.
sbh1.3:43.19: When, having approached [a sight], with prior thought, with prior effort, with prior intent, [there is] the seeing of forms with the eye — namely of kings, of kings’ ministers, townsmen, country-folk, brāhmaṇas, the wealthy, chiefs, caravan-leaders; or of other recluse-places, of huts, of pavilions, of stalls, of palaces, of mansion-stories;
sbh1.3:43.20: or again, the seeing of other worldly spectacles — this is called
sbh1.3:43.22: When he rightly knows the looking-ahead and looking-around by their own-marks,
sbh1.3:43.23: [and] how one should look ahead, how one should look around — this too he rightly knows.
sbh1.3:43.24: This is called for him full awareness.
sbh1.3:43.25: He, endowed with that full awareness,
sbh1.3:43.26: if looking around, knows ‘I am looking around’;
sbh1.3:43.27: what should be looked at ahead or around, that he looks at;
sbh1.3:43.28: when one should look ahead or around,
sbh1.3:43.29: then he looks ahead, [then he] looks around;
sbh1.3:43.30: as one should look ahead or around, so he looks ahead, [so he] looks around.
sbh1.3:43.33: namely in looking ahead and looking around.
sbh1.3:43.34: What is bending, what is stretching, what is dwelling with full awareness in bending and stretching?
sbh1.3:43.35: He, thus looking ahead and looking around,
sbh1.3:43.36: preceded by setting forth and preceded by returning, whether he bends his feet or stretches [them],
sbh1.3:43.40: thus whichever limb or sub-limb he bends
sbh1.3:43.43: If he knows the bending-and-stretching by their own-marks, [and] what should be bent,
sbh1.3:43.46: when one should bend, when one should stretch — that too he rightly knows;
sbh1.3:43.47: as one should bend, as one should stretch — that too he rightly knows. This is called for him full awareness.
sbh1.3:43.48: He, endowed with that full awareness,
sbh1.3:43.53: what should be bent or stretched, that he bends [or] stretches;
sbh1.3:43.54: when one should bend [or] stretch, then he bends [or] stretches. This is called for him
sbh1.3:43.55: dwelling with full awareness, namely in bending and stretching.
sbh1.3:44.2: What is bearing robes? What is bearing the bowl? What is dwelling with full awareness in bearing saṅghāṭi, robes, [and] bowl?
sbh1.3:44.4: that uppermost robe of his — of sixty patches or of ninety patches, double-stitched or single-stitched — this is called saṅghāṭi;
sbh1.3:44.6: [and] rightly bearing it is called wearing.
sbh1.3:44.7: And that middle [robe], the smaller [robe], the base-cloth, the extra cloth —
sbh1.3:44.9: or the extra cloth that should be color-allocated [by dyeing] — these are called robes;
sbh1.3:44.11: [and] rightly bearing them is called wearing.
sbh1.3:44.12: And that vessel, of metal or earthenware, for alms-food — this is called
sbh1.3:44.13: the bowl; its [carrying is its] enjoyment,
sbh1.3:44.14: [and] rightly bearing it is called wearing [/carrying].
sbh1.3:44.15: If, [furthermore,] he rightly knows this saṅghāṭi, robe, [and] bowl, [along with their] bearing, by their own-marks;
sbh1.3:44.17: is allowable or not allowable, that too he rightly knows;
sbh1.3:44.18: when the saṅghāṭi-, robe-, [or] bowl-bearing should be borne,
sbh1.3:44.20: as it should be borne, that too he rightly knows.
sbh1.3:44.23: He, endowed with that full awareness,
sbh1.3:44.24: if he bears saṅghāṭi, robe, [or] bowl, knows ‘I am bearing [it]’;
sbh1.3:44.25: what should be borne, he bears;
sbh1.3:44.26: when it should be borne, then he bears [it];
sbh1.3:44.27: as it should be borne, so he bears [it]. This is called for him dwelling with full awareness,
sbh1.3:44.28: namely in bearing saṅghāṭi, robe, [and] bowl.
sbh1.3:44.33: What is dwelling with full awareness in eating, drinking, chewing, [and] tasting?
sbh1.3:44.34: Whatever alms-food enjoyment [there is] — all that is called ‘eaten.’
sbh1.3:44.35: Its further division is twofold: chewed and tasted.
sbh1.3:44.37: barley-meal or cakes, rice porridge, or some other prepared food — variously cooked, edible, life-sustaining — this is called chewed [i.e.,] eaten-but-not-drunk.
sbh1.3:44.39: Namely milk, curd, butter, ghee, oil, honey, syrup, meat, fish, dried meat, salt, forest-fruit, or [other] kinds of edibles — this is called tasted, eaten but not drunk.
sbh1.3:45.1: What is drunk: candied juice, sugary juice,
sbh1.3:45.2: rice-water, curd-whey, sour gruel, buttermilk, or even water —
sbh1.3:45.4: If he rightly knows what is eaten, drunk, chewed, [and] tasted by their own-marks;
sbh1.3:45.5: [and] what should be eaten, drunk, chewed, [or] tasted — that too he rightly knows;
