sbh1.3:47.1: What is the sequence and cultivation of dwelling with full awareness? When someone here, depending on whichever village or market-town he dwells in,
sbh1.3:47.3: ‘This village or market-town is to be approached by me for alms.
sbh1.3:47.4: Having gone for alms, I should return again to the dwelling.
sbh1.3:47.6: in this village or town families that are not to be approached by me.
sbh1.3:47.9: the brothel, the tavern, the prostitute, the royal household, the caṇḍāla execution-ground,
sbh1.3:47.10: or families wholly hostile [or] not [worth] returning to.
sbh1.3:47.11: And there are families to be approached by me —
sbh1.3:47.12: namely, kṣatriya-mahāsāla families, brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla families, market-town families, country families, wealthy families, chief families, [and] caravan-leader families — [these] are to be approached, but not too late in the evening,
sbh1.3:47.13: not at the wrong time, not when the donor-patrons are busy with work, not when [they are] engaged in play or pleasure or adornment, not when devoted to village-affairs, not when angry.
sbh1.3:47.14: And I should approach in such a way that, approaching, I would not encounter a raging elephant, a raging horse, a fierce horse, a fierce cow, [or] a fierce dog; would not tread on dense undergrowth or thorny barricades,
sbh1.3:47.15: would not fall into a pit, a muddy pool, a precipice,
sbh1.3:47.16: not into refuse-water, not into cesspits. Like the moon I should approach the families,
sbh1.3:47.17: possessing moral shame, non-brazen, withdrawn in body, withdrawn in mind, not desiring gain, not desiring honor.
sbh1.3:47.18: As I am clear-minded [and] glad at my own gain, so I should be clear-minded [and] glad at another’s lack-of-gain or gain — non-self-aggrandizing, non-other-deprecating,
sbh1.3:47.19: of compassionate mind, of pitying mind.
sbh1.3:47.20: And thus again I should approach.
sbh1.3:47.21: How is this to be obtained by one gone forth, [going] in others’ families — that others should give me, or not give, [and so on] up through swiftly, not slowly,’ [as elaborated] above.
sbh1.3:47.22: ‘Having approached, in receiving [I] should observe due measure,
sbh1.3:47.23: and not for the sake of gain should I make hypocrisy;
sbh1.3:47.24: talkative chatter, insinuation, extortion, gain-seeking-by-gain should not be made;
sbh1.3:47.25: and that gain should be enjoyed unattached,
sbh1.3:47.26: unclinging, ungreedy, unbinding, unbeguiled, unfixated, [and] not fallen into fixation.
sbh1.3:47.27: And [as for] those forms which in approaching or having approached are [normally] to be seen,
sbh1.3:47.28: only some of those are to be looked at;
sbh1.3:47.29: toward those not [proper] to be seen, one should be with eyes [merely] raised,
sbh1.3:47.30: with well-collected senses; toward those that are [proper] to be seen, [one should be] with well-established mindfulness.
sbh1.3:47.31: What kind of forms are not to be looked at?
sbh1.3:47.32: Namely: a dancer, a comedian, a jester,
sbh1.3:47.33: or another obscuring [performer] engaged in dance, song, music;
sbh1.3:47.34: likewise especially a young, fine-complexioned, lust-arousing woman — and [in general] those forms whose seeing would harm the holy life, would be an obstacle to the holy life, would conduce to the manifestation of evil, unwholesome thoughts.
sbh1.3:47.35: What kind of forms are to be seen?
sbh1.3:47.36: Namely: the aged, old, decrepit, of wheezing breath, of forward-bowed body, leaning on a staff, of trembling body; or one afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, with swollen feet, swollen hands, swollen belly, swollen face, pale, eczema-ridden, scabies-ridden, leprous, suffering, of struck-down limbs;
sbh1.3:47.37: or [one] dead, time-gone, one-day dead, two-days dead, seven-days dead,
sbh1.3:47.38: devoured by crows, ospreys, vultures, dogs, [or] jackals, eaten by various animal-creatures; or [a corpse being] carried — placed on a bier with canopy spread above, with a great crowd behind, weeping, lamenting, with hair scattered and loosed, in sorrow, in suffering,
sbh1.3:47.40: in dejection, in distress — these are what should be seen; and other such forms are to be seen,
sbh1.3:47.41: [namely] those that conduce to the support of the holy life and to the manifestation of wholesome thoughts.
sbh1.3:47.42: One should not approach with shaking body, shaking arms, shaking head; not with raised voice; not with arm-grasping, not with shoulder-shaking, not without permission.
sbh1.3:47.43: One should not sit on a seat
sbh1.3:47.44: without examining the seat; not laying the whole body upon it, not [with] foot on foot, not [with] thigh on thigh, not [with] feet contracted, not [with] feet spread, not with [the body] covered up, not [in a] high-handed [manner], not with fingers spread, not cross-legged — having put on the robe round about, not too high, not too low, not on the side of the chin, not as a palmyra-fan, not as a snake-board.
sbh1.3:47.45: One should not cover [the bowl] with a porridge-lump; one should not present the bowl when food is not yet brought, nor [act improperly] with regard to chewable and edible [items];
sbh1.3:47.46: one should not place the bowl on uncovered ground or in a precipitous, sloping place; the alms-food should be enjoyed in proper measure.
sbh1.3:47.47: One should not cover the soup with rice,
sbh1.3:47.48: [nor] enjoy [it] with the soup engaged on the rice — [eating] not too thick, not too thin, with round morsels of food,
sbh1.3:47.49: not licking the hand, not licking the bowl,
sbh1.3:47.50: not slurping the hand, not slurping the bowl,
sbh1.3:47.51: not breaking [up] the morsel — [thus] alms-food should be enjoyed.
sbh1.3:48.1: ‘And when I have returned to the dwelling from those families, having come and again gone out, by day or by night, I should walk on a private walking-path,
sbh1.3:48.3: [on one] not entrusted [to others], uninvited [by others to use], unallotted [to others]; with body unfatigued, body unwearied, with mind restrained from agitation, applied to the wholesome side, following [the practice of] non-attention [to distractions], with faculties turned inward, with mind not going outward, not too swiftly, not too restlessly, not solely engaged in going-and-returning — going from time to time, standing from time to time. Thus in his own dwelling,
sbh1.3:48.4: in his own group, in his own hut, in the appointed place, the private place — not in another’s place, [which is] not entrusted, uninvited — thus on couch or stool or grass-mat, in forest or at the foot of a tree or [in an] empty hut, one should sit,
sbh1.3:48.5: folding the legs cross-wise, having set the body upright, having established mindfulness facing forward. In the middle watch of the night one should sleep,
sbh1.3:48.6: and the day-prior watch [i.e., the first night-watch] should be passed in the wholesome side,
sbh1.3:49.1: perceiving light, mindful, fully aware, attending to the perception of rising. In the last watch of the night, lightly very lightly waking, application should be made to study or recitation,
sbh1.3:49.2: or to abandonment, retreat, [or] Dharma-reflection — and the worldly-doctrine mantras should be avoided,
sbh1.3:49.3: [those] of varied letters, varied words and phrases, connected with meaninglessness, which lead not to higher knowledge, not to awakening, not to nirvāṇa.
sbh1.3:49.4: Those dharmas, however, spoken by the Tathāgata, deep, of deep appearance, connected with emptiness, conforming to this-conditioned-arising — those should be grasped with respect,
sbh1.3:49.5: firmly, stably, well grasped, not destroyed,
sbh1.3:49.6: for the accomplishment of [meditative] practice, not for gain and honor;
sbh1.3:49.7: and those dharmas should be well mastered by voice.
sbh1.3:49.8: And one should not pass time in company, in love of work, in love of speech; from time to time, with established mindfulness, having met co-religionists, one should speak with them, converse, awaken them — being of the inquiring sort, a seeker of what is wholesome,
sbh1.3:50.1: of non-grasping mind, of measured speech, of suitable speech, of calm speech.
sbh1.3:51.1: Having spoken a Dharma-talk to others, in the desire for silence, evil unwholesome thoughts should not be excessively entertained,
sbh1.3:51.2: and one should not be applied to unwise dharma-reflection.
sbh1.3:51.3: Thus many dharmas of this kind have been grasped by him,
sbh1.3:51.4: retained, well mastered by voice, examined by mind,
sbh1.3:51.7: How is he an attainer [of meditative states]?
sbh1.3:51.8: He becomes a gainer of the perception of impermanence, of the perception of suffering in the impermanent, of the perception of non-self in suffering, of the perception of revulsion toward food, of the perception of the bloody, of the perception of the scattered, of the perception of the bone, [and] of the perception that reviews emptiness.
sbh1.3:51.10: of the first dhyāna, [the] second, third, [and] fourth; of the sphere of infinity of space, infinity of consciousness, nothingness, neither-perception-nor-non-perception; of loving-kindness, compassion, [sympathetic] joy, [and] equanimity; of the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, [and] of the two-sphere [super-]knowledge; of past-life knowledge, divine ear, decease-and-rebirth knowledge, mind-reading, arhatship, [and] the eight liberations of meditation.
sbh1.3:51.12: and competent to admonish others by the three wonders:
sbh1.3:51.13: the wonder of psychic power, the wonder of mind-reading, the wonder of admonition.
sbh1.3:51.16: Toward others he is full of compassion,
sbh1.3:51.17: full of pity, desirous of their welfare,
sbh1.3:51.18: desirous of their benefit, [their] ease, [their] ease-of-contact, [their] security from bondage.
sbh1.3:51.20: How is he of unwearying mind?
sbh1.3:51.21: He becomes a shower of delight,
sbh1.3:51.22: an exhorter, a gladdener, an arouser, a knower of the four assemblies, skilled in Dharma-teaching, non-lazy, endowed with [the capacity for] rising,
sbh1.3:51.23: of aroused energy, of aroused-energy nature.
sbh1.3:51.24: Thus he is of unwearying mind.
sbh1.3:51.26: Abused, he does not abuse in return;
sbh1.3:51.27: angered [against], he does not anger in return;
sbh1.3:51.28: disputed against, he does not dispute [back];
sbh1.3:51.29: disparaged, he does not disparage [in return].
sbh1.3:51.30: Through such [reciprocal] giving-and-receiving-of-blows, he becomes equanimous; even in deep bondage, imprisonment, beating, threatening, [or] cutting, he [counts] himself at fault,
sbh1.3:51.31: and follows up the result of [his prior] action;
sbh1.3:51.32: he is not angry with others,
sbh1.3:51.33: nor does he bear a latent tendency [of anger].
sbh1.3:51.34: Thus disregarded, deprecated, [or] despised, he does not falter,
sbh1.3:51.35: has no [other] intention than [for] the goal — and he is patient
sbh1.3:51.36: of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, gnats, mosquitoes, wind, sun, creeping creatures, [patient] of ill-spoken [words] from others, of ill-arrived [hardships], of falling-out [strife]; of bodily painful feelings — intense, harsh, sharp, disagreeable, life-threatening — he is patient, of accommodating nature.
sbh1.3:52.3: in an assembly he teaches Dharma
sbh1.3:52.4: with unfaltering voice, without lapse of mindfulness or [of] inspiration;
sbh1.3:52.5: and on account of [his] confidence, no fear of [losing] confidence arises in him, comes upon him; nor does sweat from trembling pour from him, nor from disease-weariness.
sbh1.3:52.7: How is he endowed with the speech-faculty?
sbh1.3:52.8: He is endowed with noble speech:
sbh1.3:52.9: sweet, articulate, clear, pleasing to hear, agreeable, non-clinging, sufficient.
sbh1.3:52.10: Thus he is endowed with the speech-faculty,
sbh1.3:52.12: He, endowed with these eight causes, becomes an admonisher,
sbh1.3:52.13: a reminder, an advisor, an instructor, [and] a Dharma-teacher.
sbh1.3:53.2: Namely, [for failure] in higher virtue by [pointing out] virtue-failure, in misconduct by [pointing out] conduct-failure, he admonishes by what is seen, by what is heard, by what is suspected,
sbh1.3:53.3: by what is real, not by what is unreal; in [proper] time, not out of time; connected with meaning, not unconnected with meaning; gently, not harshly; with friendliness, not with hostility.

sbh1.3:53.7: or of the Dharma, or of its meaning.

sbh1.3:53.9: When someone who has fallen into a transgression [no longer] remembers [it],

sbh1.3:53.13: When someone, alone, [tries to] recall the dharmas [previously] heard, grasped —

sbh1.3:53.25: and what is wholesome, connected with meaning, connected with the holy life,
sbh1.3:53.26: long since done, long since spoken — of that too he reminds.
sbh1.3:53.29: In [matters of] seclusion, retreat, yoga, mental engagement, [and] calm-and-insight, from time to time he sets in motion appropriate admonition,
sbh1.3:53.30: and from time to time engages in connected talk —
sbh1.3:53.31: namely, talk that leads to the dispelling of hindrances of the mind: virtue-talk, wisdom-talk, liberation-talk, talk of few-desires, talk of the knowing-and-seeing of liberation, contentment-talk, abandonment-talk, dispassion-talk, cessation-talk, decrease-talk, non-mixing-talk, [and] this-conditioned-arising-conforming talk.
sbh1.3:53.34: Being the teacher in the dispensation of the well-instructed Teacher [in matters of] Dharma and Vinaya,
sbh1.3:53.35: or [being] a preceptor, or a co-religionist, or a guru, or a person occupying the place of a guru — in any matter of [the disciple’s] overstepping or transgression, knowing of it,
sbh1.3:53.36: from time to time he chastens [him],
sbh1.3:53.39: and again, by Dharma, at the [proper] time he accepts [his] conciliation, propriety, [and] resolution;
sbh1.3:53.41: in what should be done and not done, in good conduct and misconduct, in conducted and unconducted [matters] — he instructs and disciplines. Thus he is an instructor.
sbh1.3:53.43: From time to time he gives the preliminary-action talk —
sbh1.3:53.44: namely, [the talks on] generosity, virtue, heaven, the danger in sense-pleasures, the escape, [and on] the dharmas on the side of purification, [all] of which he proclaims in detail.
sbh1.3:53.45: From time to time he gives talk connected with the four noble truths,
sbh1.3:53.46: [talk] taking up suffering, origin, cessation, [and] fruit — for the maturation of beings, for their de-defilement, for their purification, for the long endurance of the true Dharma — with suitable words and letters, accompanied [by the right context], conforming [to the audience], conforming to the occasion, suitable, befitting, auspicious, equipped with the limbs and requisites of alert mindfulness; and he gives that talk at the [proper] time,
sbh1.3:53.48: gladdening, pleasing, encouraging, not depressing — suitable, accompanied [appropriately], unscattered, in accord with Dharma, in accord with the assembly, of friendly mind, beneficial mind, compassionate mind,
sbh1.3:53.49: not depending on gain, honor, [or] praise; he does not exalt himself,
sbh1.3:53.50: [and] does not deprecate others. Thus he is a Dharma-teacher.
sbh1.3:53.51: He who is endowed with these eight aspects [admonisher, reminder, advisor, instructor, Dharma-teacher, etc.]
sbh1.3:53.52: and is thus from time to time an admonisher, reminder,
sbh1.3:53.53: advisor, [and] instructor — therefore he is called a good friend [kalyāṇa-mitra].

sbh1.3:53.61: namely, taking up that very conferral of welfare-and-ease,
sbh1.3:53.62: [then,] wholly perfect by these four causes,
sbh1.3:53.63: he is in brief to be understood as the good friend.
sbh1.3:53.64: And this is the summary meaning of association with good friends.

sbh1.3:60.19: the hearing of the true dharma.
sbh1.3:60.21: When someone here is a sūtra-bearer (*sūtra-dhara*),
sbh1.3:60.23: or a mātṛkā-bearer, or a sūtra-vinaya-bearer, or a sūtra-abhidharma-bearer, or a vinaya-mātṛkā-bearer —
sbh1.3:60.24: this is called hearing of the true dharma.
sbh1.3:60.27: hearing of the letter and hearing of the meaning.
sbh1.3:60.29: When someone here, alone and secluded, [takes up] those very dharmas as heard —
sbh1.3:60.30: having set aside the six matters that are unthinkable (namely: reflection on self, on the being, on the world, on the karmic-results of beings, on the meditator's domain accessible only to meditators, and on the Buddha's domain accessible only to Buddhas) — he reflects on them by their own characteristic
sbh1.3:60.32: That reflection, again, is twofold: by way of enumeration (joined with the enumeration-procedure for dharma),
sbh1.3:60.33: and by way of weighing (by reasoning, examining merits and faults).
sbh1.3:60.34: If he reflects on the aggregate-connected teaching.
sbh1.3:60.35: If he reflects on some particular previously-settled teaching, by these two he reflects.
sbh1.3:60.38: And that form included in the dharma-sense-base — that is the form-aggregate; the three feelings are the feeling-aggregate.
sbh1.3:60.39: The six perception-bodies are the perception-aggregate.
sbh1.3:60.40: The six volition-bodies are the volition-aggregate.
sbh1.3:60.41: The six consciousness-groups are the consciousness-aggregate. Thus, by way of enumeration-and-counting, he reflects on the aggregates with progressive subdivision; the entry-procedure for this enumeration-mode of reflection is to be understood as boundless.
sbh1.3:60.42: How does he reflect on the aggregate-teaching by way of examining reasoning?
sbh1.3:60.44: Which four? Namely: the reasoning of dependence, the reasoning of cause-and-effect, the reasoning of demonstration-of-arising,
sbh1.3:61.1: What is the reasoning of dependence?
sbh1.3:61.2: Dependence is twofold: dependence-of-arising (*utpatty-apekṣā*) and dependence-of-designation (*prajñapty-apekṣā*).
sbh1.3:61.3: Of these, dependence-of-arising: the causes and conditions on which the manifestation of the aggregates depends.
sbh1.3:61.4: In that arising of the aggregates, those causes and conditions are depended upon.
sbh1.3:61.5: [Dependence-of-designation:] the sequences of names, words, and letters on which the designation of the aggregates depends.
sbh1.3:61.6: In that designation of the aggregates, those sequences of names, words, and letters are depended upon.
sbh1.3:61.7: This is called dependence-of-arising in the aggregates
sbh1.3:61.10: and whichever is the dependence-of-designation — that is the reasoning, the procedure, the means
sbh1.3:61.12: and aggregate-designation; therefore it is called the reasoning of dependence.
sbh1.3:61.13: Reasoning of cause-and-effect: the engagement of the so-arisen aggregates, by means of their own cause and their own condition, in their respective proper functions — for example:
sbh1.3:61.14: by the eye, forms are to be seen;
sbh1.3:61.15: by the ear, sounds are to be heard;
sbh1.3:61.16: and so on up to: by the mind, dharmas are to be cognized.
sbh1.3:61.17: [Conversely:] by form, [one's seeing] should rest in the eye's range;
sbh1.3:61.18: by sound, in the ear's range; and so on through dharmas in the mind's range —
sbh1.3:61.19: and whatever else is of this kind.
sbh1.3:61.20: Wherever, among the dharmas, the mutual cause-and-effect counterparts thus apply — that procedure, that means — is called
sbh1.3:61.22: What is the reasoning of demonstration-of-arising?
sbh1.3:61.23: [The propositions:] ‘the aggregates are impermanent, dependently arisen, suffering, empty, non-self’ — these he examines by three means of valid cognition: namely, trusted scripture, direct perception, and inference.
sbh1.3:61.24: By these three demonstration-yoked means of valid cognition, which grip the hearts of the wise, delineation and demonstration are made —
sbh1.3:61.25: namely, of the impermanence, dependent-arising-ness, suffering, and emptiness of the aggregates. This is called the reasoning of demonstration-of-arising.
sbh1.3:61.26: What is the reasoning of dharma-nature?
sbh1.3:61.27: By what reason are these aggregates as they are, the world-arrangement as it is? By what reason is earth marked by hardness, water by fluidity, fire by heat, wind by motion?
sbh1.3:61.28: [By what reason are] the aggregates impermanent, [and] by what reason is nirvāṇa peaceful?
sbh1.3:61.30: feeling by experiencing, perception by conceiving, formations by forming, consciousness by cognizing.
sbh1.3:61.31: This is the nature of these dharmas; their own-nature is just this.
sbh1.3:61.32: This is dharma-nature, and this very dharma-nature itself
sbh1.3:61.33: is the reasoning, the procedure, the means here.
sbh1.3:61.34: [Whether one asks:] Could this be so,
sbh1.3:61.35: or otherwise, or not at all — in every case, dharma-nature alone is the reasoning, [the explanation that] falls back on dharma-nature itself.
sbh1.3:61.36: [It serves] for the mind to contemplate, for the mind to assent — this is called the reasoning of dharma-nature.
sbh1.3:61.37: Thus by these four reasonings the aggregate-teaching is examined.
sbh1.3:61.38: And whatever other teaching too — when, by these two modes (enumeration and examining-by-reasoning) it is rightly contemplated — that teaching's [contemplation] is called
sbh1.3:62.4: What follows will state the inward and outward *obstacles*;
sbh1.3:62.7: What, then, is the inward obstacle?
sbh1.3:62.8: When someone has previously made merit,
sbh1.3:62.9: and by the well-doneness of those merits is now a gainer
sbh1.3:62.10: — from time to time — of life-conforming requisites,
sbh1.3:62.11: namely robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, and provisions: in the very midst of these, intense and prolonged lust arises,
sbh1.3:62.14: Or, again, he has previously committed actions that lead to illness,
sbh1.3:62.15: by which he is now full of illness —
sbh1.3:62.16: in this very life he moves about in an unbalanced way;
sbh1.3:62.17: his wind, bile, phlegm, or cholera frequently rises and persists in his body.
sbh1.3:62.19: of much business, much to do, frequently in large gatherings.
sbh1.3:62.20: Or fond of work, fond of speech, fond of sleep, fond of company,
sbh1.3:62.21: or self-aggrandizing, fickle, heedless, dwelling in a bad place.
sbh1.3:62.22: Such are the inward obstacles, to be understood.
sbh1.3:62.24: Even so, when he depends on non-good persons
sbh1.3:62.25: from whom he does not, from time to time, gain conforming admonition and instruction;
sbh1.3:62.26: or when he dwells in a bad region —
sbh1.3:62.27: where, when he tries to settle in to dwell, by day there is a fierce, abundant sun-glare,
sbh1.3:62.29: loud noise, the clamor of a great crowd;
sbh1.3:62.30: or sharp contact of wind and sun, or even fear of humans — such are the outward obstacles, to be understood.
sbh1.3:62.31: Such, then, is the detailed division.
sbh1.3:63.3: the obstacle of application (*prayoga*), the obstacle of seclusion (*prāvivekya*),
sbh1.3:63.5: Of these, the obstacle of application: that obstacle which, when present and manifest, makes him incapable and unfit — completely, entirely — for any application to the wholesome side.
sbh1.3:63.7: When he becomes afflicted, gravely ill — his wind, bile, phlegm, or cholera frequently rising and persisting in his body;
sbh1.3:63.8: or when a scorpion bites him, or a centipede, or a human harasses him, or a non-human;
sbh1.3:63.9: or when he is not a gainer of robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, and provisions — such is the obstacle of application, to be understood.
sbh1.3:63.10: What is the obstacle of seclusion?
sbh1.3:63.11: When he becomes [over-]heavy in food, of much business, much to do, much to attend to; when he becomes fond of work and delights in it,
sbh1.3:63.12: his mind bent on those various duties;
sbh1.3:63.13: when he becomes fond of speech,
sbh1.3:63.15: for seclusion, abandonment, retreat, and cultivation, he is content with mere recitation and study, fond of sleep,
sbh1.3:63.16: seized by sloth-and-torpor, of lazy disposition, cherishing the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of [lying on the] side, the pleasure of reclining;
sbh1.3:63.17: when he becomes fond of company with householders and renouncers,
sbh1.3:63.19: or thief-talk, food-talk, drink-talk, gossip about possessions, courtesans, streets, the countryside, tales about great ministers, sea-stories —
sbh1.3:63.20: passing the time with such useless talk,
sbh1.3:63.21: delighting in it, frequently in large gatherings,
sbh1.3:63.22: his mind scattered over those various matters,
sbh1.3:63.24: when he becomes fond of association,
sbh1.3:63.25: and when separated from those householders and renouncers he undergoes separation-grief;
sbh1.3:63.26: when he becomes fond of conceptual proliferation,
sbh1.3:63.27: delighting in proliferation — a leader in things to be plunged into, but in matters of seclusion one who has laid down the burden —
sbh1.3:63.28: such are the dharmas to be understood as the obstacle of seclusion:
sbh1.3:63.29: [dharmas] by which, when present and manifest, it is not easy to dwell in remote lodgings in forests and woods,
sbh1.3:63.30: or at the foot of trees, or in empty huts.
sbh1.3:63.31: What is the obstacle of retreat?
sbh1.3:63.33: There is the obstacle of calm
sbh1.3:63.35: Of these, the obstacle of calm [comes from two things:] heedlessness and dwelling in a bad place.
sbh1.3:63.36: When, in the heedless, sloth-and-torpor wraps the mind round,
sbh1.3:63.38: or inclines the mind toward slackness,
sbh1.3:63.39: or there is a darkened state of mind —
sbh1.3:63.40: and as for [obstacles arising] from dwelling in a bad place,
sbh1.3:63.41: by some human conflict from outside [interfering].
sbh1.3:63.42: And what is the obstacle of insight?
sbh1.3:63.44: Of these, self-aggrandizement: when [he thinks] ‘I am of high family, gone forth,
sbh1.3:63.46: and others are not so,’ he exalts himself,
sbh1.3:63.49: Likewise [thinking], ‘I am gone forth from a wealthy family, undejected; I am handsome, well-favored, pleasing; I am much-learned, of much accumulation;
sbh1.3:63.50: I am of fair speech, endowed with the faculty of speech — and other monks are not so’ —
sbh1.3:63.54: Holding himself up [thus, he thinks of others:] ‘these
sbh1.3:63.55: monks, elders, knowers-of-delight, ones who have descended into the holy life’ — and so he does not, from time to time, inquire of them,
sbh1.3:63.57: And they, in turn, do not from time to time open up to him the unopened places,
sbh1.3:63.58: do not lay open the unopened places,
sbh1.3:63.59: do not — by wisdom, well and rightly — penetrate and proclaim
sbh1.3:63.60: the deep meaning-words to him, [which would lead] up through the purification of knowledge-and-vision.
sbh1.3:63.64: Further, when he gains only a slight, scant, mere knowledge-and-vision, a mere meaningful ease of contact,
sbh1.3:63.66: that mere vision, he exalts himself,
sbh1.3:63.68: and being thus self-aggrandizing, is content with that much and does not strive further —
sbh1.3:63.69: thus too an obstacle is made for him
sbh1.3:63.70: through self-aggrandizement: namely, an obstacle to insight.
sbh1.3:63.71: Or, again, fickle — of unpeaceful faculties,
sbh1.3:63.74: speaking what is well-spoken yet doing what is ill-done — he does not firmly reflect on the dharmas,
sbh1.3:63.76: By this he does not bring insight to fullness, does not purify it — thus fickleness too
sbh1.3:63.79: [In sum:] two dharmas are obstacles to calm —
sbh1.3:63.80: namely, heedlessness and dwelling in a bad place.
sbh1.3:63.81: Two dharmas are obstacles to insight — namely, self-aggrandizement and fickleness.
sbh1.3:63.82: Whatever is the obstacle to calm,
sbh1.3:63.83: and whatever is the obstacle to insight —
sbh1.3:63.84: this together is called the obstacle to retreat.
sbh1.3:63.85: And this is the summary meaning of obstacle.
sbh1.3:63.87: together with the previous detailed division —
sbh1.3:63.89: And by the reverse of this obstacle, *non-obstacle* is to be understood:
sbh1.3:63.90: the absence, departure, non-presence, and non-occurrence of these obstacles is what is called *non-obstacle*.
sbh1.3:64.2: That blameless gift which one gives for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of refining the mind, for the sake of the requisites of yoga, and for the attainment of the highest good.
sbh1.3:64.3: Here [the structure of the analysis is]: who gives, to whom does one give, what does one give, by what does one give,
sbh1.3:64.6: by [answering all of] which, his giving becomes blameless.
sbh1.3:65.3: [The one who] is called *giver* (*dātṛ*) is whose own thing is given;
sbh1.3:65.4: [the one who] is called *patron* (*dāna-pati*) is one who gives
sbh1.3:65.5: by his own desire to give, not unwillingly.
sbh1.3:65.6: And to whom does one give?
sbh1.3:65.8: one gives to four [kinds of recipient]:
sbh1.3:65.12: the pitiable, travelers, beggars, the blind, the deaf, the helpless, those without recourse, those lacking life-requisites —
sbh1.3:65.14: Helpers are: mother and father, those who nurture and rear one,
sbh1.3:65.15: or those who deliver one from a forest-wilderness, from famine, from fear of enemy armies, from bondage,
sbh1.3:65.16: or from sickness; and those who counsel one's welfare,
sbh1.3:65.17: counsel one's ease, bring about welfare and ease, help in matters that have arisen, share one's joys, share one's sorrows, and do not abandon one in danger — these and others of such kind are the helpers.
sbh1.3:65.21: love, respect, or devoted speech — those one greets, knows well, holds beloved —
sbh1.3:65.22: and others of such kind. These are called the dear.
sbh1.3:66.2: Recluses and brahmins reckoned as good —
sbh1.3:66.3: the unafflicted, those who delight in the unafflicted; the lust-free and those practicing for the subduing of lust; the hatred-free and those practicing for the subduing of hatred;
sbh1.3:66.4: the delusion-free and those practicing for the subduing of delusion.
sbh1.3:66.5: These and others of such kind are called the distinguished.
sbh1.3:67.2: In brief, one gives a thing reckoned as either sentient or non-sentient.
sbh1.3:67.5: Namely the giving of son, female slave, male slave, worker, attendant, elephant, horse, cow, sheep, fowl, woman, man, boy, or girl —
sbh1.3:67.7: Or with respect to one's own body — hand, foot, head, flesh, blood, fat, and so on — he offers these.
sbh1.3:67.8: This [self-giving] too is a sentient-reckoned gift, [the kind] in which bodhisattva-awakenings are visible;
sbh1.3:67.9: but it is not the gift intended in the present context.
sbh1.3:67.10: [Here intended is rather:] all those [sentient beings] over whom he has lordship,
sbh1.3:67.12: and whom he is fit to bestow on others.
sbh1.3:67.13: Bestowing them, he makes himself blameless:
sbh1.3:67.14: [the gift is given in such a way that] others do not corrupt their minds on its account, by way of its condition;
sbh1.3:67.15: and those beings bestowed on others are not afflicted by them — this is called the blameless gift of sentient-things.
sbh1.3:68.4: Of these, wealth-things: gems, pearls, beryl, conch-shell, stone, coral, agate, gold, silver, copper, right-spiraling [shells];
sbh1.3:68.5: or any other such jewel, gold, silver, cloth, vessel or furniture, fragrance, or garland — this is called wealth.
sbh1.3:68.7: Whatever is food or drink: barley, rice, wheat, jujube, horse-gram, sesame, beans, sugar-cane juice, grape juice — or any other such thing. This is called grain.
sbh1.3:69.2: Namely: a field, a house, a shop, the establishment of a merit-hall or a monastery —
sbh1.3:69.3: or any other such thing. This is called land-thing.
sbh1.3:69.4: [All of these] — the sentient-reckoned thing and the [non-sentient-reckoned thing] — these are what one gives.
sbh1.3:70.2: By volition accompanied by non-greed — that is, mental conditioning, mental action —
sbh1.3:70.3: and by the bodily action produced therefrom,
sbh1.3:70.4: and the verbal action, for the relinquishment of [whatever] thing, [whether external] or in one's own continuum:
sbh1.3:70.8: with received tradition as one's view, seeing the fruit, one gives respectfully;
sbh1.3:70.9: with humble mind, with one's own hand, with both hands;
sbh1.3:70.10: without contempt, at the right time;
sbh1.3:70.11: in such a way that the gift will be of use to others, without injuring [those others] in the giving;
sbh1.3:70.12: by dharma, by proper means, without violence — having accumulated [the gift] rightly, one gives what is pure,
sbh1.3:70.13: what is fine, what is allowable;
sbh1.3:70.14: [gives in such a way] that others are not made blameworthy [by accepting it],
sbh1.3:70.15: nor is oneself [made blameworthy by giving it];
sbh1.3:70.17: having disciplined the stain of stinginess and the stain of hoarding, one gives the gift;
sbh1.3:70.18: with glad mind before the giving, with mind clarified during the giving,
sbh1.3:70.19: and one is not remorseful afterward.
sbh1.3:70.24: namely, to the suffering; out of gratitude —
sbh1.3:70.25: namely, to the helpers; with love, respect, and devotion —
sbh1.3:70.26: namely, to the dear; with the prayer for worldly and otherworldly distinction —
sbh1.3:70.29: [in this way alone] is it said that ‘one gives.’
sbh1.3:70.30: By these modes — for him, whether householder or renouncer — for the sake of adorning the mind, for the sake of refining the mind,
sbh1.3:70.31: for the sake of the requisites of yoga, for the attainment of the highest good, that gift becomes blameless.
sbh1.3:71.1: What is the ornament of the recluse [śramaṇālaṅkāra]?
sbh1.3:71.2: When someone here is of faith,
sbh1.3:71.4: of little affliction, of aroused-energy nature, wise, of few desires, content,
sbh1.3:71.5: easily maintained, easily supported, endowed with ascetic qualities [dhutaguṇa], pleasing, knowing measure,
sbh1.3:71.6: endowed with the dharmas of noble persons,
sbh1.3:71.7: endowed with the dharmas of the wise,
sbh1.3:71.8: endowed with the marks of the wise,
sbh1.3:72.2: Full of serenity [śraddhā as confident clarity],
sbh1.3:72.3: full of meaning-imagining [conviction in the value of the goal],
sbh1.3:72.4: full of release-aspiration, and willing in wholesome dharmas.
sbh1.3:72.5: He is serene toward the Teacher,
sbh1.3:72.12: having honored, esteemed, respected, [and] worshiped, depending on him, he dwells [in practice].
sbh1.3:72.13: As toward the Teacher, so toward the Dharma,
sbh1.3:72.14: toward co-religionists, toward the training, toward admonition-and-instruction, toward conciliation, toward heedfulness, toward concentration — thus he is of faith.
sbh1.3:72.16: He is straight, of straight nature;
sbh1.3:72.17: he reveals himself as he truly is
sbh1.3:72.18: in the presence of the Teacher, the wise, [and his] co-religionists — thus he is non-deceitful.
sbh1.3:72.19: How is he of little affliction?
sbh1.3:72.21: he is endowed with an evenly-conditioned stomach,
sbh1.3:72.22: not too hot, not too cold, unafflicted, naturally pleasant, by [the function of] which his eaten, drunk, chewed, [and] tasted [foods] are properly digested — thus he is of little affliction.
sbh1.3:72.23: How is he of aroused-energy nature?
sbh1.3:72.25: with energy, enthusiastic, of firm valor,
sbh1.3:72.26: not one who has laid down the burden in wholesome dharmas — skilled, not lazy, endowed with [the capacity for] rising;
sbh1.3:72.28: of bodily service for [his] wise co-religionists — thus he is of aroused energy.
sbh1.3:72.30: He is endowed with both mindfulness and intellect,
sbh1.3:72.31: of non-dull faculty, non-deluded faculty, alert, capable of understanding the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken dharmas,
sbh1.3:72.35: How is he of few desires?
sbh1.3:72.36: Endowed with however many qualities — beginning with the state of few-desires — he does not seek to be known by others [for them]:
sbh1.3:72.37: ‘Let others not know me as of few desires, or as endowed with such qualities.’ Thus he is of few desires.
sbh1.3:72.39: With whatever robes, alms-food, [or] lodging [he obtains], he is satisfied, content; whether obtaining inferior or fine robes, he does not long [for more],
sbh1.3:72.41: and having obtained, he enjoys [them] unattached,
sbh1.3:72.43: As with robes, so with alms-food [and] lodging. — How is he easily maintained?
sbh1.3:72.44: Only he himself is to be maintained by him,
sbh1.3:72.45: not others — such as children or [household] men,
sbh1.3:72.46: or others on whose account he would undertake seeking [more],
sbh1.3:72.47: and [whom] other donor-patrons would [come to] see as ‘hard to maintain.’
sbh1.3:72.48: Not [being] thus, he is easily maintained.
sbh1.3:72.50: Even with little he gets along,
sbh1.3:72.51: even with inferior he gets along — thus he is easily supported.
sbh1.3:72.52: How is he endowed with ascetic qualities?
sbh1.3:72.55: a one-seat eater [aikāsanika], an after-meal-only refuser [khalupaścādbhaktika],
sbh1.3:72.56: a three-robe wearer [traicīvarika], a felt-wearer [nāmatika], a refuse-rag wearer [pāṁsukūlika],
sbh1.3:72.57: a forest-dweller [āraṇyaka], a tree-root dweller [vṛkṣamūlika], an open-air dweller [ābhyavakāśika],
sbh1.3:72.58: a cemetery dweller [śmāśānika], a sitter [naiṣadika, one who does not lie down],
sbh1.3:72.60: These [are] the twelve ascetic qualities, with reference to alms-food, robes, [and] lodging —
sbh1.3:72.62: [Counted as thirteen,] the alms-food-taker quality, when divided, becomes twofold:
sbh1.3:72.63: the [plain] alms-food-taker [who eats] as obtained, and the sequential alms-food-taker who, having gone [house-to-house, even at] prostitute-and-attendant families, having wandered, enjoys the alms-food as obtained, as suitable — not approaching families with raised expectation [thinking]:
sbh1.3:72.64: ‘There I shall obtain fine chewable, edible, suitable [food].’
sbh1.3:72.65: When alms-food-taking is taken without distinction [as a single quality], they become twelve;
sbh1.3:72.66: when the [twofold] division is taken, thirteen.
sbh1.3:72.68: Seated in one [single] seat, however much should be enjoyed,
sbh1.3:72.70: once risen from that seat, he does not [again] enjoy [food the same day].
sbh1.3:73.2: Seated for a meal, he does not [begin to] enjoy [it]
sbh1.3:73.3: until he has accepted all the food,
sbh1.3:73.4: [i.e.,] until he knows ‘I shall be able to maintain myself [with this much]’;
sbh1.3:73.5: when he knows ‘beyond this no further food shall be needful for me,’
sbh1.3:73.6: then, having put aside everything [else, refusing more], he begins
sbh1.3:73.8: Thus he is an after-meal refuser.
sbh1.3:73.9: How is he a three-robe wearer?
sbh1.3:73.10: With [just] three robes he gets along — saṅghāṭi, upper robe, [and] inner robe;
sbh1.3:73.11: he does not hold [/keep] more than three robes — thus he is a three-robe wearer.
sbh1.3:75.2: three robes or extra robes — all that he wears is wool [/felt],
sbh1.3:75.5: How is he a refuse-rag wearer [pāṁsukūlika]?
sbh1.3:75.6: Whatever robe has been left by others,
sbh1.3:75.7: discarded — on the road, in the lane, at the crossroads, at a junction, on the path or off-path; mixed with feces, mixed with urine, [or] mingled with feces, urine, pus, blood, [or] mucus —

sbh1.3:75.10: He dwells in remote forest-thicket lodgings,
sbh1.3:75.11: those distant from villages and market-towns — thus he is a forest-dweller.
sbh1.3:76.1: How is he a tree-root dweller [vṛkṣamūlika]?
sbh1.3:76.2: He makes his abode at the foot of a tree,
sbh1.3:76.4: Thus he is a tree-root dweller. — How is he a cemetery dweller [śmāśānika]?
sbh1.3:76.5: He makes his abode in a cemetery, [the place] where the dead are
sbh1.3:76.6: carried out — thus he is a cemetery dweller.
sbh1.3:77.2: On couch, stool, [or] grass-mat, he passes the time [only] by sitting,
sbh1.3:77.3: not leaning his back or side against a couch, stool, wall, tree-root, grass-mat, or leaf-mat — thus he is a sitter.
sbh1.3:77.4: How is he an any-bed acceptor [yāthāsaṁstarika]?
sbh1.3:77.5: Wherever — on grass-mat or leaf-mat — he prepares the bed:
sbh1.3:77.6: whatever grass-mat or leaf-mat has been once arranged,
sbh1.3:77.7: just so he uses [it as] the bed,
sbh1.3:77.9: he [merely] arranges [it as it is] — thus he is an any-bed acceptor.
sbh1.3:77.10: Why are these called ‘ascetic qualities’ [dhutaguṇa, lit. ‘shaken-off qualities’]? Namely, just as wool or cotton, when shaken [dhuta], becomes loose,
sbh1.3:77.11: and at that time is soft,
sbh1.3:77.12: light, [and] workable — namely for spinning thread or for stuffing cotton —
sbh1.3:77.13: just so, for someone here, by lust for alms-food the mind is attached to alms-food,
sbh1.3:77.14: joined together [with it]; [and] by lust for robes, lust for lodging, the mind is attached,
sbh1.3:77.16: He, by these ascetic qualities, purifies [it], straightens [it],
sbh1.3:77.17: makes [it] soft, workable, straightforward, controllable — namely for the dwelling of the holy life; therefore they are called ‘ascetic qualities.’
sbh1.3:78.1: Now, for the abandonment of lust for plentiful food in alms-food, he becomes a one-seat eater.
sbh1.3:78.2: For the abandonment of lust for plentiful food, he becomes an after-meal refuser.
sbh1.3:78.3: For the abandonment of lust for fine [/soft] robes, he becomes a felt-wearer.
sbh1.3:78.4: For the abandonment of lust for fine [/many] robes, he becomes a three-robe wearer.
sbh1.3:78.5: For the abandonment of lust for soft-contact robes, he becomes a refuse-rag wearer.
sbh1.3:78.11: Now, for the abandonment of contact-lust, he becomes a forest-dweller.
sbh1.3:78.12: For the abandonment of shelter-lust, he becomes a tree-root dweller [or] an open-air dweller,
sbh1.3:78.14: Moreover, cemetery-dwelling is [also] for the abandonment of lust [arising] through torpor.
sbh1.3:78.15: For the abandonment of lust for side-pleasure [or] lying-pleasure, he becomes a sitter.
sbh1.3:78.16: For the abandonment of lust for spread, coverlet, [and] covering, he becomes an any-bed acceptor. — Thus he is endowed with ascetic qualities.
sbh1.3:78.18: He is endowed with pleasing setting-forth-and-returning, looking ahead, looking around, bending and stretching, [and] wearing of saṅghāṭi, robes, [and] bowl — thus he is pleasing.
sbh1.3:78.19: How is he knowing the right measure?
sbh1.3:78.20: When faithful brāhmaṇa-householders provide for him as one gone forth —
sbh1.3:78.21: namely with robes, alms-food, lodging, medicine, [and other] requisites — in receiving them, he knows the measure.
sbh1.3:78.22: Thus he is knowing the right measure.
sbh1.3:78.23: How is he endowed with the dharmas of noble persons?
sbh1.3:78.24: Gone forth from a high family, or from a wealthy family, handsome, well-favored to see, pleasing, much-learned, endowed with abundant requisites,
sbh1.3:78.25: [or being] a gainer of some kind of mere knowledge, mere vision, [or] mere meaningful ease-of-contact — by these he does not exalt himself,
sbh1.3:78.27: he is practiced for the Dharma-conformity of Dharma — thus he is endowed with the dharmas of noble persons. — How is he endowed with the marks of the wise?
sbh1.3:78.28: The fool is action-marked, [and] the wise [too] is action-marked.
sbh1.3:78.29: How [so]? The fool is an ill-thought-out thinker,
sbh1.3:78.30: an ill-spoken speaker, an ill-done-doer. The wise, on the other hand, is a well-thought-out thinker,
sbh1.3:78.32: Thus he is endowed with the marks of the wise.
sbh1.3:78.34: Abused, he does not abuse in return;
sbh1.3:78.35: angered [against], he does not anger in return;
sbh1.3:78.37: reviled, he does not revile in return.
sbh1.3:78.39: Of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, gnats, mosquitoes, wind, sun, [and] creeping creatures’ contacts; of ill-spoken [words] from others, of ill-arrived [hardships], [and] of [hostile] paths of speech;
sbh1.3:78.40: of bodily feelings — painful, intense, harsh, biting, disagreeable, life-threatening — he is patient, of accommodating nature.
sbh1.3:78.43: When [he is] endowed with friendly bodily action,
sbh1.3:78.44: with friendly verbal action, [and] friendly mental action — in the presence of the Teacher, the wise, [and his] co-religionists — [being] a sharer of common enjoyments and not a separate-enjoyer,
sbh1.3:78.45: he is an open-eater [/sharer at meals],
sbh1.3:78.46: with gains lawful, Dharma-obtained, [whatever is] bowl-gone or bowl-included [he shares]; [he is] sharing in virtue
sbh1.3:78.48: He, endowed with these six conciliatory dharmas — dear-making, esteem-making, dwelling-stable-making — becomes pleasant to live with,
sbh1.3:78.50: and the wise rejoice in him,
sbh1.3:78.55: Free from frowning, of open-faced complexion, accompanied by a smile, the first to greet,
sbh1.3:78.60: He, endowed with these dharmas, is desirous of Dharma,
sbh1.3:78.62: not desirous of gain, honor, fame, [or] eulogy.
sbh1.3:78.63: He is not endowed with the wrong view of superimposing [what does not exist],
sbh1.3:78.64: nor with [the wrong view] of depreciating [what does exist];
sbh1.3:78.65: what is not the Dharma he does not superimpose [onto Dharma],
sbh1.3:78.66: what is the Dharma he does not depreciate.
sbh1.3:78.68: spoken — talked — [in the form of] letters, signs, words [connected] with worldly-doctrine,
sbh1.3:78.70: knowing thus, he avoids [it] from afar;
sbh1.3:78.71: he does not delight in it, does not take pleasure in it; on this account he bears his own self-administered ascetic vow [/robe].
sbh1.3:78.76: He does not make [overly close] friend-families,
sbh1.3:78.78: [knowing:] ‘on account of which there will arise, in many modes, scatter [and] busyness; or, through their further change, [their] becoming otherwise, will arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, distress.’
sbh1.3:78.79: And the defilements and secondary defilements as they arise he does not accommodate,
sbh1.3:78.80: [but] abandons, dispels, [and] puts an end to [them],
sbh1.3:78.81: [thinking:] ‘lest from that, on that account, there arise either present-life suffering or future-life suffering.’
sbh1.3:78.82: And he does not let the [donors’] arising of faith fall away [through misconduct].
sbh1.3:78.84: of unfallen vow, he enjoys what is given in faith,
sbh1.3:78.85: and he does not reject what is given in faith;
sbh1.3:78.87: He is a seeker of his own faults and slip-ups,
sbh1.3:78.88: a concealer of [his own] good, a revealer of [his own] evil.
sbh1.3:78.89: In others’ faults and slip-ups he does not engage; he does not fall into transgression,
sbh1.3:78.90: [not] even for the sake of [his] life;
sbh1.3:78.91: and if fallen, lightly very lightly he makes amends according to Dharma.
sbh1.3:78.92: In duties to be done he is skilled, non-lazy, a self-doer, not seeking bodily service from others.
sbh1.3:78.93: And the inconceivable greatness of the Buddhas and Buddha-disciples, and the deep teaching, he resolves on,
sbh1.3:78.95: ‘The Tathāgatas alone are the knowers, seers, beholders — not I.’
sbh1.3:78.96: Having seen thus, he does not himself become a view-clinger, a wrong-grasper, [or] one ill-relinquishing-counsel.
sbh1.3:78.97: He, endowed with these qualities, so dwelling, so training, adorned with the ornament of the recluse, shines — just as some young man of vital nature, an enjoyer of sense-pleasures, bathed and anointed,
sbh1.3:78.100: namely with necklaces, bracelets, ring on the finger, or garland of gold and silver —
sbh1.3:78.101: just so he, adorned with the various recluse-ornament qualities,
sbh1.3:78.103: Therefore it is called ornament of the recluse.
sbh1.3:78.104: This is called the ornament of the recluse.
sbh1.3:80.2: food, wakefulness, dwelling with full awareness,
sbh1.3:81.1: and likewise hearing-and-reflection on the true dharma,
sbh1.3:81.2: non-obstacle, generosity, and the ornament [of the recluse] last.
sbh1.3:82.1: Faith, non-deceit, little affliction, energy, wisdom, few desires, contentment, ease of being cared for,
sbh1.3:83.1: ease of support, the ascetic qualities, knowing-measure, patience, gentleness, refinement.
sbh1.3:84.1: [Here ends] the first yoga-position, comprised within the Śrāvakabhūmi of the Yogācārabhūmi.
